title: Verb 'to be' (am / is / are)
explanation: Use am with I, is with he/she/it, are with you/we/they. Wrong: 'She are tired.' Right: 'She is tired.'

lesson.whatItIs: 'Be' is the most common verb in English. In the present it has three forms: am, is and are. We use it to say who or what something is, and to describe people, places, feelings and states.
whenToUse: Names, jobs and nationality: 'I am a receptionist.'
Descriptions and feelings: 'The room is cold.' 'We are tired.'
Age and location: 'She is 70.' 'The bag is at the desk.'

form.example: I am late. / I'm late.
She is from Japan. / She's from Japan.
They are guests. / They're guests.
He isn't here. We aren't ready.
Is the lift working? Are you okay?
I was tired. They were outside.

examples: I'm the new receptionist.
The rings aren't in the box.
Is Mr. Weller in his room?
We were at the mast at noon.

commonMistakes.why: Adjectives need 'be' before them in English.
'Agree' is already a verb, so don't add 'am'.
Use only one form of 'be' in a question.

tips: Use contractions (I'm, she's, they're) in chat; they sound natural.
Don't put 'be' before normal verbs: 'I work', not 'I am work'.

title: Present simple
explanation: For habits, facts and routines. Add -s/-es with he/she/it. Wrong: 'He work here.' Right: 'He works here.'

lesson.whatItIs: The present simple describes things that are always true, habits, routines and timetables. The verb is in its base form, but with he/she/it you add -s or -es.

form.example: They work at the villa.
She works at the villa.
watch → watches, go → goes
carry → carries
He doesn't work today.

form.pattern: Question: Do / Does + subject + base verb?
form.example: Does she work here?

examples: The manager checks the cash every morning.
I don't drink coffee at night.
How often do you check the radio?
Kofi fixes everything.

commonMistakes.why: After does/doesn't, use the base verb; the -s moves to 'does'.
Don't add 'am' before a present simple verb.

tips: have → has with he/she/it: 'She has a key.'
Common time words: always, usually, every day, on Mondays.

title: Subject-verb agreement
explanation: The verb must match its subject in number. Wrong: 'The guests is waiting.' Right: 'The guests are waiting.'

lesson.whatItIs: The verb must agree with its subject: a singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Mistakes happen most when the subject is long or far from the verb.
whenToUse: Every present-tense sentence, especially with be, have and present simple verbs
Long subjects: 'The list of guests is...'

form.example: The guest is angry. The guest wants a refund.

form.pattern: Plural subject + are / have / base verb
form.example: The guests are angry. The guests want a refund.
The key to the rooms is lost. (subject = key)
Everyone is here. Each room has a safe.
Hana and Mateo are outside.

examples: The list of guests is wrong.
My parents live in Lagos.
Nobody knows where the rings are.
The police are coming. ('police' is always plural)

commonMistakes.wrong: The box of rings are empty.
commonMistakes.right: The box of rings is empty.

commonMistakes.why: After 'there', the verb matches the noun that follows.

tips: Ask 'who or what is doing this?' to find the real subject.
news, information and luggage are singular: 'The news is bad.'

title: A vs an
explanation: Use 'an' before a vowel sound, 'a' before a consonant sound. Wrong: 'a hour', 'an university'. Right: 'an hour', 'a university'.

lesson.whatItIs: A and an mean 'one'. Use them before singular countable nouns when you mention something for the first time or don't mean a specific one. The choice between a and an depends on the first sound, not the first letter.
whenToUse: Any one of many: 'Can I have a towel?'

form.example: a bag, a room, a university ('you' sound)
an hour (silent h), an engineer, an umbrella
a big problem, an old watch

form.pattern: Not with plurals or uncountable nouns
form.example: bags (not 'a bags'), water (not 'a water')

examples: I need an answer.
He's an honest man.
It's a one-way street. ('one' starts with a 'w' sound)
Can I get a taxi?
tips: Say the word aloud and listen to the first sound, not the letter.
The next word decides: 'an old bag' but 'a bag'.

title: Using 'the' or no article
explanation: Use 'the' for something specific or already known; no article for general plurals and uncountables. Wrong: 'I need the help.' Right: 'I need help.' / 'Where is the key you gave me?'

lesson.whatItIs: 'The' is used when the listener knows exactly which thing you mean. When you talk about things in general, use no article with plural or uncountable nouns.
whenToUse: Second mention: 'I saw a bear. The bear was huge.'
Only one exists in this context: the sun, the manager, the lift
Defined by a phrase: 'the key on the desk'
Superlatives and order: the best, the first

form.example: The lift is broken.
Bears are dangerous.
Fuel is expensive here.

form.pattern: the + noun defined by a phrase
form.example: The money in the drawer is missing.

form.pattern: No article: most countries, cities, meals
form.example: in Italy, at lunch (but the UK, the USA)

examples: The station has fuel for five days.
I love Italian food. (general)
The food at the wedding was amazing. (specific)
Call the police.

commonMistakes.why: A specific key both people know needs 'the'.
Fixed phrases: go to work, go home, go to bed.

tips: Ask: does the listener know which one? Yes → the.
General statements usually have no article.

title: Missing article
explanation: Singular countable nouns usually need a/an/the. Wrong: 'I lost bag.' Right: 'I lost my bag.' / 'I lost a bag.'

lesson.whatItIs: In English, a singular countable noun almost never stands alone. It needs a word before it: a/an, the, my/your, this/that or a number. Many languages don't need this, so it is one of the most common mistakes.
whenToUse: Every time you use a singular countable noun: bag, room, problem, flight, question

form.example: I lost a bag.
The flight is late.
My watch is missing.
This room is cold.

examples: There is a problem with my room.
Can you open the door?
She is a lawyer.
I have a question.

commonMistakes.why: 'Bag' is singular and countable, so it needs a word before it.
A singular countable noun needs a/an.

tips: Check every singular noun in your sentence: does it have a word before it?
Exceptions are fixed phrases: at home, by car, go to bed, at night.

title: Plural nouns
explanation: Regular plurals add -s/-es; learn irregular ones (person-people, child-children). Wrong: 'two bag', 'three persons came'. Right: 'two bags', 'three people came'.

lesson.whatItIs: Countable nouns change to a plural form when there is more than one. Most add -s, some add -es or change their spelling, and some common nouns are irregular.
whenToUse: After many, few, several, these, those

form.example: bag → bags, guest → guests
box → boxes, watch → watches
party → parties
knife → knives, life → lives
person → people, child → children, man → men, woman → women, foot → feet

examples: Three people are waiting.
Two of the boxes are missing.
These keys don't work.
How many guests are coming?

commonMistakes.why: After a number above one, use the plural.
The normal plural of person is people.

tips: A plural noun takes a plural verb: 'The people are...'
'One of the + plural': 'one of the guests'.

title: Subject and object pronouns
explanation: Subject: I, he, she, we, they. Object: me, him, her, us, them. Wrong: 'Me and him went.' Right: 'He and I went.'

lesson.whatItIs: Pronouns replace nouns so we don't repeat names. Subject pronouns do the action and come before the verb. Object pronouns receive the action and come after a verb or a preposition.
whenToUse: 'It' for things and animals; 'they' for plurals or a person whose gender you don't know

form.pattern: Subject: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
form.example: She called me.

form.pattern: Object: me, you, him, her, it, us, them
form.example: I called her.
with me, for them, to him

form.pattern: Two people as subject: put yourself last
form.example: Grace and I checked the room.

examples: Tobias is angry. He wants a room.
Can you help us?
Give it to them.
Hana and I are at the mast.

commonMistakes.why: Subjects need subject pronouns; put yourself last.
After a preposition, use the object form.

commonMistakes.wrong: My sister she is a doctor.
commonMistakes.why: Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun.

tips: Test it: remove the other person. 'Me went' sounds wrong → 'I went'.
Never use 'it' for a person.

title: Possessive adjectives, pronouns and 's
explanation: my/your/his/her/its/our/their before a noun; mine/yours after; 's for owners. Wrong: 'the bag of Mateo', 'This is my.' Right: 'Mateo's bag', 'This is mine.'

lesson.whatItIs: Possessives show who something belongs to. Use possessive adjectives before a noun, possessive pronouns on their own, and 's after a name or noun.
whenToUse: Ownership, relationships and parts: my husband, the hotel's lift

form.pattern: my / your / his / her / its / our / their + noun
form.example: This is her watch.

form.pattern: mine / yours / his / hers / ours / theirs (no noun after)
form.example: The watch is hers.
Mateo's data, the guest's bag
the guests' rooms

form.pattern: its (belongs to it) vs it's (= it is)
form.example: The hotel and its staff. It's late.

examples: Is this your bag or mine?
Amara's mother is here.
Their flight is cancelled.
The station lost its power.

commonMistakes.why: Without a noun, use the possessive pronoun.

commonMistakes.wrong: She lost his watch. (her own watch)
commonMistakes.why: His/her matches the owner, not the object.

tips: his = belongs to a man; her = belongs to a woman. Think about the owner.
Never add an apostrophe to possessive pronouns: yours, hers, its, theirs.

title: Question word order
explanation: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb. Wrong: 'Where you are going?' Right: 'Where are you going?'

lesson.whatItIs: English questions change the word order: an auxiliary verb (do, does, did, is, are, can, will, have) comes before the subject. Question words (where, what, when, why, how) go at the very start.

form.example: Is the lift working?

form.pattern: Other verbs: Do / Does / Did + subject + base verb?
form.example: Did you see the rings?
Where did you put it?

form.pattern: Modals: Can / Will / Should + subject + verb?
form.example: Can you help me?

form.pattern: When who/what is the subject: no do/did
form.example: Who took the money?

examples: What time does the plane leave?
Why are you late?
How much fuel do we have?
Who called the technician?

commonMistakes.why: The auxiliary comes before the subject.

commonMistakes.right: What time does the plane leave?

commonMistakes.why: Put the auxiliary + n't before the subject.
When 'who' is the subject, don't use 'did'.

tips: Remember QUASI: Question word, Auxiliary, Subject, Infinitive (verb).
In casual chat 'You're okay?' works, but learn the full form.

title: Negatives with don't / doesn't
explanation: Use don't/doesn't + base verb in present simple negatives. Wrong: 'She don't know.' / 'He doesn't knows.' Right: 'She doesn't know.'

lesson.whatItIs: To make a normal verb negative, use don't or doesn't + the base verb in the present, and didn't + the base verb in the past. 'Be' and modal verbs (can, will, should) just add 'not'.
whenToUse: Saying something is not true or not happening

form.pattern: I / you / we / they + don't + verb
form.example: They don't know.
He doesn't know.
She didn't take it.

form.pattern: Be: am not / isn't / aren't / wasn't / weren't
form.example: It isn't here.
I can't find it.

examples: The generator doesn't work.
I don't understand.
We didn't see a bear.
You mustn't go out alone.

commonMistakes.why: After doesn't, use the base verb (no -s).
After didn't, use the base verb.

tips: The -s or -ed moves to the auxiliary: works → doesn't work, worked → didn't work.
Never use two negatives: 'I don't know nothing' → 'I don't know anything'.

title: Prepositions of time (in / on / at)
explanation: at + clock time, on + days/dates, in + months/years/parts of the day. Wrong: 'on 5 PM', 'in Monday'. Right: 'at 5 PM', 'on Monday'.

lesson.whatItIs: At, on and in show when something happens. Choose by how specific the time is: at for exact times, on for days and dates, in for longer periods.

form.example: at 5 PM, at night
on Monday, on 5 May, on my birthday

form.pattern: in + month / year / season / part of day
form.example: in June, in 2026, in winter, in the morning

form.pattern: No preposition: today, tomorrow, yesterday, next, last, this, every
form.example: I'll call tomorrow. See you next week.

examples: The ceremony is at 5:30.
The flight leaves on Friday.
We arrived in the evening.
I'll check again in ten minutes. (= after ten minutes)

commonMistakes.why: Parts of the day → in (but 'at night').
No preposition before next / last / this.

tips: Think of a pyramid: in (big periods) → on (days) → at (exact points).
'In time' = early enough; 'on time' = exactly when planned.

title: Prepositions of place (in / on / at)
explanation: in + enclosed spaces/cities, on + surfaces/floors, at + points/addresses. Wrong: 'in the 3rd floor'. Right: 'on the 3rd floor'.

lesson.whatItIs: In, on and at show where something is. In = inside a space or area, on = on a surface or a level, at = at a point or a place where an activity happens.
whenToUse: Describing where people and things are

form.example: in the lift, in Lisbon, in the box
on the table, on the 3rd floor, on the plane

form.pattern: at + point / address / event / place of activity
form.example: at the desk, at the wedding, at the airport

form.pattern: Other: under, next to, between, behind, in front of
form.example: next to the boathouse

examples: The watch was in the laundry.
Your key is on the desk.
I'm at reception.
The bear is behind the mast.

commonMistakes.why: A point or service place → at.
Buses, trains, planes → on (but in a car or taxi).

tips: Car and taxi: in. Bus, train, plane, boat: on.
'at home', 'at work', 'at school' have no 'the'.

title: There is / there are
explanation: There is + singular/uncountable, there are + plural. Wrong: 'There is two problems.' / 'It has a problem with the room.' Right: 'There are two problems.' / 'There is a problem with the room.'

lesson.whatItIs: There is / there are says that something exists or is present. Use it to introduce new information. The verb matches the noun that comes after it.
whenToUse: Introducing something for the first time
Saying how many of something exist

form.example: There is a problem. There is some fuel.
There are two guests.
There aren't any rooms.
Is there a doctor?
There was a storm.

examples: There's a bear near the mast!
There are 120 guests, not 92.
Is there any jollof rice on the menu?
There wasn't enough time.

commonMistakes.wrong: It has a problem with my room.
commonMistakes.right: There is a problem with my room.
commonMistakes.why: To say something exists, use 'there is', not 'it has'.
Don't use 'have' to show something exists.

commonMistakes.wrong: There are a lot of luggage.
commonMistakes.right: There is a lot of luggage.

tips: First introduce with 'there is', then describe with 'it': 'There's a bag. It's black.'
In speech people say 'there's' with plurals, but write 'there are'.

title: Imperatives (instructions)
explanation: Base verb for instructions, 'Don't' + verb for negative ones. Wrong: 'You to stay calm.' / 'No open the door.' Right: 'Stay calm.' / 'Don't open the door.'

lesson.whatItIs: The imperative gives instructions, orders, warnings and advice. Use the base verb with no subject. For negative instructions, use Don't + base verb.

form.example: Stay calm. Walk south.
Don't open the door.
Please wait here.
Let's check the log.

examples: Take cover now!
Hold the torch, please.
Don't run.
Call me when you're inside.
tips: With guests or managers, soften instructions: 'Could you please...'
In emergencies, short imperatives are the clearest.

title: Spelling
explanation: The word is spelled incorrectly. Wrong: 'recieve', 'tommorow', 'definately'. Right: 'receive', 'tomorrow', 'definitely'.

lesson.whatItIs: A spelling mistake is a correct word written with the wrong letters. English spelling is irregular, so a few rules help, and the most common difficult words are worth memorising.
whenToUse: Every written message, especially formal ones

form.example: believe, receive

form.pattern: Short vowel + one consonant: double it before -ed / -ing
form.example: stop → stopped, plan → planning
make → making, write → writing
try → tried, carry → carries

examples: Commonly misspelled: tomorrow, necessary, definitely, separate, receive, accommodation, beginning, until
tips: Keep a personal list of words you often misspell.
UK and US spellings are both fine (colour/color, organise/organize). Just be consistent.

title: Punctuation and capital letters
explanation: Start sentences and names with capitals, write 'I' as a capital, and end questions with '?'. Wrong: 'i am from lisbon. can you help me.' Right: 'I am from Lisbon. Can you help me?'

lesson.whatItIs: Punctuation and capital letters make writing clear and professional. Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark.
whenToUse: All writing, especially messages to managers or clients

form.pattern: Capital at the start of a sentence
form.example: The lift is broken.

form.pattern: Capitals for I, names, places, days, months, languages
form.example: I met Inês in Lisbon on Monday.

form.pattern: ? at the end of a direct question
form.example: Can you help me?
It was late, but she called.
don't, it's, Amara's

examples: Hello, Mr. Weller. Your room is ready.
I'm from Lisbon. Where are you from?

commonMistakes.why: 'I' and place names always take a capital.
Days and months take a capital.

tips: People often skip capitals in casual chat, but practise correct writing here.
Read your message once before sending.

title: Have / have got (possession)
explanation: Use have/has (or have got/has got) for possession, family and features; questions and negatives with 'have' use do/does. Wrong: 'I have not a key.' / 'Do you have got...?' Right: 'I don't have a key.' / 'Have you got a key?'

lesson.whatItIs: We use 'have' to talk about things we own, family, illnesses and features. In British English, 'have got' means the same thing in the present. The two forms make questions and negatives differently.
whenToUse: Family and relationships: 'She has two sons.'
Features and illnesses: 'He has blue eyes.' 'I have a headache.'

form.pattern: I / you / we / they have; he / she / it has
form.example: She has a key.
I don't have a receipt.
Do you have a booking?

form.pattern: have got / has got (UK, present only)
form.example: I've got a problem.
I haven't got a key. Have you got a pen?
I didn't have a ticket.

examples: Do you have your confirmation number?
Mrs. Tanaka has a gold watch.
We haven't got much fuel.
I didn't have time to call.

commonMistakes.right: I don't have a key. / I haven't got a key.

commonMistakes.wrong: Do you have got a pen?
commonMistakes.right: Have you got a pen? / Do you have a pen?

commonMistakes.wrong: I had got a bag yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: 'Have got' is only used in the present.

tips: For actions, use 'have', not 'have got': have breakfast, have a shower, have a meeting.
American English prefers 'have' and 'Do you have...?'

title: This / that / these / those
explanation: this/these = near, that/those = far; this/that + singular, these/those + plural. Wrong: 'This keys are mine.' Right: 'These keys are mine.'

lesson.whatItIs: Demonstratives point to things. 'This' and 'these' are for things near you; 'that' and 'those' are for things further away. 'This' and 'that' are singular; 'these' and 'those' are plural.
whenToUse: Introducing people or yourself on the phone: 'This is Grace.'
Referring to something just said: 'That's a good idea.'

form.example: This bag is heavy.
These keys are mine.
That man is the manager.
Those guests are angry.
Is this yours? That's right.
this morning, that night

examples: This is my colleague, Rafael.
Are those your bags?
That was a long night.
I don't like this idea.
tips: 'That' also refers to something just mentioned: 'That's terrible!'
'These days' = nowadays; 'in those days' = in the past.

title: Question words (who, what, where, when, why, how...)
explanation: Choose the right question word: who (person), what (thing), where (place), when (time), why (reason), how (way), which (choice), whose (owner). Wrong: 'How is your name?' Right: 'What is your name?'

lesson.whatItIs: Question words ask for specific information. Each one asks for a different kind of answer, so the wrong word confuses the listener.
whenToUse: Any question that can't be answered with yes or no

form.example: Who called?
What happened?
Where is the key?
When does the plane leave?
Why are you late?
How did it happen? How are you?

form.pattern: which = choice from a small group
form.example: Which room is yours?
Whose bag is this?
How long have you waited?

examples: What's your confirmation number?
Which option do you prefer?
Whose watch is it?
How often do you check the radio?

commonMistakes.why: To ask about the owner, use 'whose'.
Don't forget the auxiliary (see question word order).

tips: 'What... like?' asks for a description: 'What's the hotel like?'
Use 'which' when there are a few choices and 'what' when the choice is open.

title: Would like (polite wants and offers)
explanation: Use 'would like' to ask for things and to make offers politely; follow it with a noun or to + verb. Wrong: 'I would like go.' / 'Do you like a drink?' (offer) Right: 'I'd like to go.' / 'Would you like a drink?'

lesson.whatItIs: 'Would like' means 'want', but it is more polite. Use it to order, request and offer. 'I'd like' is the short form.

form.example: I'd like a room for two nights.
I'd like to speak to the manager.
Would you like some water?
Would you like to sit down?

form.pattern: Would you like me to...? (offer help)
form.example: Would you like me to call a taxi?
Yes, please. / No, thank you.

examples: I'd like a receipt, please.
Would you like to file a complaint?
We'd like to move the ceremony.
What would you like to eat?

commonMistakes.why: 'I like' = general taste; 'I'd like' = a request now.

commonMistakes.wrong: Would you like some tea? — Yes, I would like.
commonMistakes.why: This is the short, natural answer.

commonMistakes.wrong: Do you like a drink? (as an offer)

tips: 'I want' can sound rude to staff; 'I'd like' is safer.
'Would you like me to...?' is the standard way to offer help.

title: Short answers (Yes, I do / No, it isn't)
explanation: Answer yes/no questions with yes/no + subject + the auxiliary from the question. Wrong: 'Do you have a key? — Yes, I have.' Right: 'Yes, I do.'

lesson.whatItIs: In English, just 'yes' or 'no' can sound cold. Short answers repeat the subject and the auxiliary verb from the question, which sounds natural and polite.

form.pattern: Do / Does → Yes, I do / No, she doesn't
form.example: Do you work here? — Yes, I do.

form.pattern: Did → Yes, I did / No, I didn't
form.example: Did you see it? — No, I didn't.

form.pattern: Be → Yes, it is / No, they aren't
form.example: Is he angry? — Yes, he is.

form.pattern: Can / Will → Yes, I can / No, I won't
form.example: Can you help? — Yes, I can.

form.pattern: Have (perfect) → Yes, I have / No, I haven't
form.example: Have you called? — Yes, I have.

examples: Are you the new receptionist? — Yes, I am.
Is there any fuel? — Yes, there is.
Did Rafael call? — No, he didn't.
Will you tell her? — Yes, I will.

commonMistakes.wrong: Do you have a key? — Yes, I have.
commonMistakes.why: Repeat the auxiliary from the question (do).

commonMistakes.wrong: Did she call? — Yes, she does.
commonMistakes.why: Match the tense of the question.

commonMistakes.wrong: Is it ready? — Yes, it does.
commonMistakes.why: Use the same verb as the question.

tips: Negative short answers can be contracted: 'No, I'm not.' 'No, it isn't.'
Add information after the short answer: 'Yes, I did. I saw it at 3 PM.'

title: Present continuous
explanation: am/is/are + -ing for actions happening now or temporary situations. Wrong: 'I wait for you now.' Right: 'I'm waiting for you now.'

lesson.whatItIs: The present continuous describes actions happening now or around now, and temporary situations. It is also used for future plans that are already arranged.
whenToUse: Happening now: 'The bear is walking towards you.'
Temporary situations: 'I'm staying at the Albatross this week.'
Arranged future plans: 'We're leaving at six.'

form.example: I'm waiting. She's coming.

form.pattern: Negative: am not / isn't / aren't + verb-ing
form.example: She isn't listening.

form.pattern: Question: Am / Is / Are + subject + verb-ing?
form.example: Are you coming?
make → making, stop → stopping, lie → lying

examples: Mateo is playing the guitar again.
Why are you laughing?
The storm is getting worse.
Luca isn't answering his phone.

commonMistakes.why: An action happening now → present continuous.
'Understand' is a state verb (see stative verbs).

tips: Time words: now, right now, at the moment, today, this week.
Present simple = always; present continuous = now: 'I work nights, but today I'm working days.'

title: Stative verbs in continuous form
explanation: Verbs like know, want, like, need, believe are not normally used in -ing form. Wrong: 'I am knowing him.' Right: 'I know him.'

lesson.whatItIs: Stative verbs describe states (thoughts, feelings, possession, senses), not actions. They are normally not used in the -ing form, even when you talk about right now.
whenToUse: Describing what you know, think, feel, want or own

form.pattern: Thinking: know, believe, understand, remember, mean
form.example: I know the answer.

form.pattern: Feelings: like, love, hate, want, need, prefer
form.example: I need a room.
This bag belongs to me.

form.pattern: Senses and appearance: seem, look like, smell, taste
form.example: It smells good.

form.pattern: Some verbs have an action meaning too
form.example: I have a key (state) / I'm having dinner (action)

examples: I need a room for tonight.
Do you remember the code?
This bag belongs to Mrs. Tanaka.
We're having a meeting. (action, so -ing is fine)

commonMistakes.why: 'Know' is a state, not an action.

tips: If you can't physically 'do' it, it is probably a state verb.
'I think it's late' (opinion) vs 'I'm thinking about it' (process) are both correct.

title: Past simple: regular verbs
explanation: Add -ed for finished past actions. Wrong: 'Yesterday I call the hotel.' Right: 'Yesterday I called the hotel.'

lesson.whatItIs: The past simple describes finished actions at a specific time in the past. Regular verbs add -ed, and the same form is used for every subject.
whenToUse: Finished actions with a past time: yesterday, last night, at 3 PM, two days ago
A sequence of events in a story

form.example: call → called, check → checked
arrive → arrived
try → tried

form.pattern: Short vowel + one consonant: double it
form.example: stop → stopped, plan → planned
walked /t/, called /d/, wanted /ɪd/

examples: I checked the log at midnight.
The lift stopped at 2:07.
She cried when she saw the watch.
We planned the menu last week.

commonMistakes.why: A finished past time needs the past form.
Double the final consonant after a short vowel.
Don't add 'was' to a past simple verb.

tips: 'Ago' goes after the time: 'two hours ago'.
In a story, keep all finished actions in the past.

title: Past simple: irregular verbs
explanation: Irregular verbs have special past forms (go-went, take-took, find-found). Wrong: 'I losed my watch.' Right: 'I lost my watch.'

lesson.whatItIs: Many common verbs don't add -ed in the past. Their past forms must be learned. The good news: the same form is used for all subjects.
whenToUse: The same situations as the regular past simple: finished past actions

form.pattern: go → went, come → came, leave → left
form.example: We left at 7.

form.pattern: take → took, give → gave, find → found, lose → lost
form.example: Grace found the watch.

form.pattern: see → saw, say → said, tell → told, know → knew
form.example: She told me the truth.

form.pattern: buy → bought, think → thought, bring → brought
form.example: He bought a ticket.

form.pattern: No change: put, cut, let, hit, cost
form.example: I put it on the desk.

examples: I lost my bag at the airport.
Grace found the watch.
He took 200 euros.
We left at 7.
tips: Learn verbs in groups that sound alike: buy/bought, bring/brought, think/thought.
Practise the 30 most common irregular verbs first.

title: Past simple questions and negatives
explanation: Use did/didn't + base verb. Wrong: 'Did you saw it?' / 'I didn't took it.' Right: 'Did you see it?' / 'I didn't take it.'

lesson.whatItIs: In past simple questions and negatives, use did / didn't. The main verb goes back to its base form, because 'did' already shows it is the past.
whenToUse: Denying or asking about finished past events

form.example: I didn't see it.
Did you see it?

form.pattern: Wh-question: Wh-word + did + subject + base verb?
form.example: Where did you put it?
Were you there?

examples: I didn't take the money.
When did you last see the watch?
Why didn't you call me?
Was the door open?
tips: Only one past form per verb phrase: did + base verb.
Short answers: 'Yes, I did.' / 'No, I didn't.'

title: Past continuous
explanation: was/were + -ing for an action in progress in the past, often interrupted. Wrong: 'I walked when the lights went out.' Right: 'I was walking when the lights went out.'

lesson.whatItIs: The past continuous describes an action that was in progress at a moment in the past. It often gives the background for a shorter action that interrupted it.
whenToUse: An action in progress at a specific past time: 'At 2 AM I was sleeping.'

form.example: I was walking. They were talking.
They weren't listening.
What were you doing at 2 AM?
I was working when the lights went out.

examples: At 2 AM I was helping Mr. Weller.
What was Rafael doing during the blackout?
While Hana was working, the bear appeared.
It was snowing all night.

commonMistakes.wrong: I walked when the lights went out.
commonMistakes.right: I was walking when the lights went out.
commonMistakes.why: The longer background action → past continuous.

commonMistakes.wrong: When I was arriving, she left.
commonMistakes.right: When I arrived, she was leaving.

tips: 'While' + long action, 'when' + short action.
Perfect for alibis: 'At 3 PM I was sitting at the desk.'

title: Future with 'will'
explanation: will + base verb for decisions made now, promises and predictions. Wrong: 'I will to call you.' Right: 'I'll call you in ten minutes.'

lesson.whatItIs: Will + base verb talks about the future when you decide at the moment of speaking, make a promise or offer, or give a prediction or opinion.
whenToUse: Predictions and opinions: 'I think it will rain.'

form.example: I'll call you.
I won't tell anyone.
Will you help me?
Shall I call a taxi?

examples: Don't worry, I'll find it.
The technician will arrive soon.
I won't be late.
Will there be jollof rice?

commonMistakes.why: After will, use the base verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: If it will rain, we'll move.
I call you later. (as a promise)

tips: 'I'll...' sounds helpful in customer service.
won't = will not.

title: Future with 'going to'
explanation: am/is/are going to + verb for plans and evidence-based predictions. Wrong: 'I going to check.' Right: 'I'm going to check.'

lesson.whatItIs: Be going to + base verb talks about plans you decided before speaking, and predictions based on what you can see now.
whenToUse: Plans and intentions: 'I'm going to call the police.'
Predictions from evidence: 'Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.'

form.pattern: am / is / are + going to + base verb
form.example: I'm going to check the log.
We aren't going to stay.

form.pattern: Question: Am / Is / Are + subject + going to...?
form.example: Are you going to tell her?
Don't write 'gonna' in formal messages.

examples: We're going to move the ceremony indoors.
He's going to miss his flight.
What are you going to say?
I'm not going to lie to you.

commonMistakes.wrong: It will rain — look at the sky!
commonMistakes.right: It's going to rain — look at the sky!

commonMistakes.wrong: I will meet her at 5. (already arranged)
commonMistakes.right: I'm meeting her at 5. / I'm going to meet her at 5.
commonMistakes.why: Arrangements → going to or present continuous.

tips: Decision now → will. Decision made before → going to.
Fixed arrangements with a time often use the present continuous.

title: Can / could for ability
explanation: can/could + base verb, no 'to' and no -s. Wrong: 'She cans help.' / 'I can to come.' Right: 'She can help.' / 'I can come.'

lesson.whatItIs: Can and could express ability. Can = present ability, could = general ability in the past. They never change form and are followed by the base verb without 'to'.

form.example: I can speak Italian.
I can't open it.
Can you swim?
We couldn't see anything.
I'll be able to help tomorrow.

examples: Kofi can fix the generator.
I can't find the rings.
Can you hear me? Over.
We couldn't see anything in the storm.

commonMistakes.right: I will be able to help.

commonMistakes.why: The modal forms the question by itself.

tips: For one specific past success, use 'was able to' or 'managed to': 'I managed to open the lift.'
'Can't' is more common than 'cannot' in speech.

title: Polite requests (could / would / may)
explanation: Use Could you...? Would you mind...? May I...? to sound polite. Wrong: 'Give me the number.' (too direct) Right: 'Could you give me the number, please?'

lesson.whatItIs: In English, direct orders can sound rude. Use modal questions and softening phrases to make requests polite, especially with guests, clients and managers.
whenToUse: Asking strangers, customers, managers, or anyone you want to be polite to

form.example: Could you check the booking?
Would you mind waiting here?

form.pattern: Can / Could / May I + base verb? (permission)
form.example: May I see your passport?

form.pattern: I'd like... / I was wondering if you could...
form.example: I was wondering if you could help me.
Could you just wait a moment, please?

examples: Could you tell me your confirmation number, please?
Would you mind spelling your name?
May I ask what happened?
Could you possibly give me a receipt?

commonMistakes.right: Could you give me the number, please?

tips: Politeness scale: Can you < Could you < Would you mind < I was wondering if you could.
Answer 'Would you mind...?' with 'No, not at all' (= yes, I'll do it).

title: Countable vs uncountable nouns
explanation: Uncountables (information, luggage, advice, furniture) have no plural and use much/a little. Wrong: 'many luggages', 'an advice'. Right: 'a lot of luggage', 'some advice'.

lesson.whatItIs: Countable nouns can be counted (one bag, two bags). Uncountable nouns can't (water, money, information): they have no plural and don't take a/an.
whenToUse: Deciding whether to use a/an, a plural, much or many

form.example: many guests, a few problems
much fuel, a little time

form.pattern: Both: a lot of, some, any, no
form.example: a lot of guests, a lot of fuel
a piece of advice, a bottle of water, two bags of luggage

examples: How much fuel is left?
How many people are coming?
Can you give me some information?
There's a lot of luggage.

commonMistakes.right: some advice / a piece of advice

tips: Uncountable words learners often get wrong: information, advice, luggage, furniture, news, equipment, money, feedback.
'Money' is uncountable, but 'euros' are countable.

title: Some / any / no
explanation: some in positive sentences and offers, any in negatives and most questions. Wrong: 'I don't have some money.' Right: 'I don't have any money.'

lesson.whatItIs: Some, any and no talk about an unspecified quantity. Use some in positive sentences, offers and requests; any in negatives and most questions; and no to mean 'not any'.
whenToUse: Talking about an amount or number you don't specify

form.example: We have some fuel.
We don't have any rooms.
Do you have any questions?
Would you like some tea?

form.pattern: no = not any (with a positive verb)
form.example: There are no rooms.
I didn't see anyone.

examples: Is there any jollof rice?
Could I have some water?
I didn't see anyone.
There's nothing in the box.

commonMistakes.right: I don't have any money. / I have no money.

commonMistakes.why: Start with 'nobody' and use a positive verb.

tips: 'Any' in a positive sentence means 'it doesn't matter which': 'Take any room.'
nobody, nothing and no are already negative.

title: Comparative adjectives
explanation: -er for short adjectives, more + long adjectives, + than. Wrong: 'more cheap', 'bigger that'. Right: 'cheaper', 'bigger than'.

lesson.whatItIs: Comparative adjectives compare two things. Short adjectives add -er; longer adjectives use 'more'. 'Than' introduces the second thing.
whenToUse: Comparing two people, things or options

form.example: cheap → cheaper, big → bigger
easy → easier, busy → busier

form.pattern: Two or more syllables: more + adjective
form.example: more expensive, more careful
good → better, bad → worse, far → further
The suite is bigger than the room.

examples: Plan B is safer than Plan A.
The boathouse is smaller, but it's drier.
Today the storm is worse than yesterday.
Could you speak more slowly?
tips: much / a lot / a bit change the size of the difference: 'much safer', 'a bit cheaper'.
as + adjective + as = equal: 'as good as'.

title: Superlative adjectives
explanation: the + -est / the most. Wrong: 'the most best', 'the biggest of the world'. Right: 'the best', 'the biggest in the world'.

lesson.whatItIs: Superlatives compare one thing with all the others in a group. Use 'the' + -est for short adjectives and 'the most' for longer ones.
whenToUse: Saying something is number one (or last) in a group

form.example: the cheapest, the biggest
the easiest
the most beautiful
good → the best, bad → the worst, far → the furthest

form.pattern: in + place / group, of + period / number
form.example: the best hotel in Lisbon, the worst day of my life

examples: This is the most important milestone.
Hana is the best medic I know.
It was the longest night of my life.
Which option is the safest?
tips: Often used with the present perfect: 'the best food I've ever eaten'.
'one of the + superlative + plural noun': 'one of the best hotels'.

title: Adverbs of frequency position
explanation: always/usually/never go before the main verb but after 'be'. Wrong: 'I go always there.' / 'He always is late.' Right: 'I always go there.' / 'He is always late.'

lesson.whatItIs: Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never) say how often something happens. Their position in the sentence follows fixed rules.

form.example: I always check the log.
He is always late.

form.pattern: Between the auxiliary and the main verb
form.example: I have never seen a bear.
Do you usually work nights?
Sometimes we lose power.

examples: Grace never forgets a room.
The generator usually works.
Mateo is always joking.
I don't often work weekends.

commonMistakes.why: The adverb goes before the main verb.

tips: Scale: always (100%) > usually > often > sometimes > rarely > never (0%).
Longer phrases (every day, twice a week) go at the end of the sentence.

title: Adjectives vs adverbs
explanation: Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs (often -ly) describe verbs. Wrong: 'Speak slow.' / 'He drives careful.' Right: 'Speak slowly.' / 'He drives carefully.'

lesson.whatItIs: Adjectives describe nouns (a careful driver). Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs (he drives carefully). Many adverbs are adjective + -ly.

form.example: slow → slowly, careful → carefully
easy → easily, happy → happily
good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard, late → late

form.pattern: After be / seem / look / feel / sound / smell: use an adjective
form.example: You look tired. That sounds good.

examples: Please speak slowly.
She handled it calmly.
He's a good negotiator. He negotiates well.
The food smells amazing.

commonMistakes.why: It describes the verb, so use an adverb.
It describes the verb, so use an adverb.
'Good' is an adjective; 'well' is the adverb.

tips: 'Hardly' means 'almost not', not 'hard': 'I hardly slept.'
'Lately' means 'recently', not 'late'.

title: Basic linking words (and / but / because / so)
explanation: because gives a reason, so gives a result, but shows contrast. Wrong: 'I was late so the taxi was slow.' Right: 'I was late because the taxi was slow.'

lesson.whatItIs: Conjunctions join ideas. And adds, but contrasts, because gives a reason, so gives a result, and or gives a choice. Choosing the wrong one changes the meaning.
whenToUse: Joining two ideas in one sentence

form.example: I called and waited.
It's small but dry.
I was late because the taxi was slow.
The taxi was slow, so I was late.
Indoors or earlier?

examples: We moved inside because it was raining.
It was raining, so we moved inside.
Luca was angry, but he agreed.
Do you want risotto or jollof?

commonMistakes.wrong: I was late so the taxi was slow.
commonMistakes.right: I was late because the taxi was slow.
I went to bed because I was tired.
commonMistakes.why: A 'because' clause can't stand alone in writing.

commonMistakes.wrong: Although it rained, but we went.
because of the taxi was slow

tips: because of + noun: 'because of the storm'.
Put a comma before 'so' and 'but' when they join two full sentences.

title: Word choice and collocations
explanation: The word exists but is wrong in this context, or does not go naturally with the other word. Wrong: 'make a photo', 'do a mistake', 'big rain'. Right: 'take a photo', 'make a mistake', 'heavy rain'.

lesson.whatItIs: Word-choice errors happen when a word is real English but wrong in this context, or doesn't naturally go with its partner word (a collocation). The grammar can be perfect and the sentence still sounds wrong.
whenToUse: Any sentence, especially when you translate from your own language

form.example: make a mistake / decision / complaint; do homework / your job / a favour
say something; tell someone something
heavy rain, strong wind, heavy traffic
lend = give for a time; borrow = take for a time
steal a thing; rob a person or a place

examples: I made a mistake.
Could you do me a favour?
She told me the truth.
Someone stole 200 euros. Someone robbed the hotel.

commonMistakes.wrong: Can you borrow me your pen?
commonMistakes.right: Can you lend me your pen?

tips: Learn words in phrases, not alone.
When unsure, search the whole phrase to see if native speakers use it.

title: Word order in a sentence
explanation: English normally uses subject + verb + object, with adjectives before nouns. Wrong: 'I like very much coffee.' / 'a bag black'. Right: 'I like coffee very much.' / 'a black bag'.

lesson.whatItIs: English word order is strict. The basic order is Subject + Verb + Object, then manner, place and time. Adjectives come before nouns, and nothing goes between a verb and its object.

form.example: I lost my bag.

form.pattern: Keep the verb and object together
form.example: I like coffee very much.
She worked quietly at the desk all night.
a black bag

form.pattern: Adjective order: opinion, size, age, colour, material
form.example: a lovely small old gold watch
big enough

examples: I saw a bear near the mast at noon.
She speaks English very well.
It's a small leather bag.
Is the room warm enough?

commonMistakes.why: Don't put words between the verb and its object.
Keep the verb and object together.

tips: Time phrases usually go at the end or the very beginning.
When a sentence feels wrong, find the subject, verb and object first.

title: Present simple vs present continuous
explanation: Present simple for habits, facts and permanent situations; present continuous for actions happening now and temporary situations. Wrong: 'I work right now.' Right: 'I'm working right now.'

lesson.whatItIs: Both tenses talk about the present, but in different ways. The present simple is for things that are always or usually true; the present continuous is for things happening now or only for a short time.
whenToUse: Habit vs now: 'I usually work days, but this week I'm working nights.'
Permanent vs temporary: 'She lives in London. She's staying in Lisbon.'

form.example: The lift stops at every floor.
The storm is getting worse.
always, usually, every day, never
now, at the moment, today, this week, currently

form.pattern: State verbs → simple even for now
form.example: I know. I need help.

examples: Kofi usually fixes things fast, but he's struggling today.
What do you do? — I'm a receptionist.
What are you doing? — I'm checking the log.
Hana works as a medic, but this week she's resting.

commonMistakes.wrong: What do you do now? (meaning: at this moment)
commonMistakes.why: 'What do you do?' asks about your job.

tips: 'What do you do?' = What's your job? 'What are you doing?' = right now.
'Always' + continuous can show annoyance: 'He's always joking!'

title: Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself...)
explanation: Use myself/yourself/himself etc. when the subject and object are the same person, or for emphasis. Wrong: 'I hurt me.' / 'They enjoyed theirselves.' Right: 'I hurt myself.' / 'They enjoyed themselves.'

lesson.whatItIs: Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject of the sentence. Use them when someone does something to themselves, or to emphasise that someone did something without help.
whenToUse: Same person as subject and object: 'She cut herself.'
Alone or without help: by myself

form.example: I hurt myself.
They introduced themselves.
She fixed it by herself.

form.pattern: Emphasis: after the noun or at the end
form.example: The manager herself called. I'll do it myself.

examples: Hana splinted her ankle herself.
Please help yourself to coffee.
Did you hurt yourself?
We had to solve it ourselves.

commonMistakes.why: Same person as the subject → reflexive.

commonMistakes.wrong: She did it by her own.
commonMistakes.right: She did it by herself. / She did it on her own.

commonMistakes.why: Don't use a reflexive as a subject.

tips: Some verbs aren't reflexive in English: relax, feel, meet, concentrate (not 'relax yourself').
'Each other' is different: 'They blamed each other' (A blamed B and B blamed A).

title: Too / enough
explanation: too + adjective = more than is good; adjective + enough = sufficient; enough + noun. Wrong: 'enough big', 'too much expensive'. Right: 'big enough', 'too expensive'.

lesson.whatItIs: 'Too' means more than is good or possible. 'Enough' means as much as needed. 'Not enough' means less than needed.
whenToUse: Explaining problems: 'The boathouse is too small.'
Saying something is or isn't sufficient: 'We don't have enough fuel.'

form.example: too cold, too slowly

form.pattern: too much + uncountable / too many + plural
form.example: too much luggage, too many guests
warm enough, fast enough
enough fuel, enough rooms
too heavy for the plane, old enough to drive

examples: The cargo is too heavy for the plane.
Is the room big enough for 120 guests?
We don't have enough time.
There are too many people in the lift.

commonMistakes.why: 'Too much' is only used before nouns.

tips: 'Too' always means a problem; 'very' is neutral.
'not big enough' = 'too small'.

title: Prepositions of movement (to, into, out of, towards...)
explanation: Movement prepositions show direction: to (destination), into (enter), out of (exit), towards, across, along, through, up/down. Wrong: 'I went in the room.' / 'Go to home.' Right: 'I went into the room.' / 'Go home.'

lesson.whatItIs: Prepositions of movement describe direction: where someone or something is going. They are different from prepositions of place, which describe where something is.

form.example: Walk to the station.
Get into the lift. Get out of the car.
The bear is walking towards you.
across the ice, along the lake, through the door
up the stairs, past the mast, around the building
Go home. Come here.

examples: Walk south towards the station.
She ran out of the room.
Take the path along the lake.
Come back inside.

commonMistakes.why: Car / taxi → get in / get out of; bus / plane → get on / get off.

commonMistakes.right: The bear is walking towards us.

tips: arrive at (a place) / arrive in (a city or country), never 'arrive to'.
Get on / off: bus, train, plane, boat. Get in / out of: car, taxi.

title: Infinitive of purpose (to + verb)
explanation: Use to + verb to explain why someone does something. Wrong: 'I came for help you.' / 'I called for to ask.' Right: 'I came to help you.' / 'I called to ask.'

lesson.whatItIs: To explain the reason for an action, English uses 'to' + base verb after the action. 'In order to' is a more formal version, and 'for' + noun also gives a purpose.

form.example: I called to ask about my bag.
We reduced heating in order to save fuel.
I came for the meeting.

form.pattern: Negative: so as not to / in order not to
form.example: Walk slowly so as not to scare it.

examples: Grace went downstairs to check the laundry.
I'm writing to confirm your booking.
We moved inside to avoid the storm.
She called the villa for an update.

commonMistakes.why: Purpose with a verb → to + verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: I study English for get a job.
commonMistakes.right: I study English to get a job.

tips: Answer 'Why?' with 'To + verb': 'Why did you go out? — To check the mast.'
'for + -ing' describes what a thing is used for: 'This kit is for treating injuries.'

title: Also / too / as well / either
explanation: 'also' goes before the main verb; 'too' and 'as well' go at the end of positive sentences; 'either' goes at the end of negative ones. Wrong: 'I don't like it too.' / 'I like also it.' Right: 'I don't like it either.' / 'I also like it.'

lesson.whatItIs: These words add information that is similar to something already said. Their position depends on the word, and in negative sentences you need 'either', not 'too'.

form.pattern: also: before the main verb, after 'be'
form.example: I also checked the log. She is also tired.

form.pattern: too / as well: end of a positive sentence
form.example: I checked the log too.

form.pattern: either: end of a negative sentence
form.example: I didn't see it either.
'I'm tired.' — 'Me too.' / 'I'm not hungry.' — 'Me neither.'

examples: Kofi also wants more fuel.
Daniel is nervous, and Amara is nervous too.
Rafael didn't help, and he didn't call either.
Bring the red kit as well.

commonMistakes.why: 'Also' usually goes in the middle of the sentence.
Agreeing with a negative → me neither.

tips: 'Me too' for positives, 'Me neither' for negatives.
Starting a sentence with 'Also,' is fine in informal lists of points.

title: Zero conditional
explanation: If/when + present simple, present simple for facts and things that always happen. Wrong: 'If you heat ice, it will melts.' Right: 'If you heat ice, it melts.'

lesson.whatItIs: The zero conditional talks about general truths, rules and things that always happen in a certain situation. Both parts use the present simple.

form.pattern: If / When + present simple, present simple
form.example: If you heat ice, it melts.
The alarm rings if the door opens.
If the light is red, don't enter.
When the power goes, the generator starts.

examples: If the temperature drops below zero, the pipes freeze.
When guests complain, we offer a free drink.
If you press this button, the lift stops.
If it rains, the terrace floods.

commonMistakes.wrong: If you heat ice, it will melts.
commonMistakes.right: If you heat ice, it melts.
commonMistakes.why: General truths use the present simple in both parts.

commonMistakes.wrong: If it rain, the terrace floods.
commonMistakes.right: If it rains, the terrace floods.

commonMistakes.wrong: If you will press the button, it stops.
commonMistakes.right: If you press the button, it stops.

commonMistakes.wrong: When water boil, it make steam.
commonMistakes.right: When water boils, it makes steam.

tips: Zero = always true; first conditional = one specific future situation.
You can replace 'if' with 'when' or 'whenever'.

title: Commonly confused words (their / there / they're...)
explanation: Words that sound alike but mean different things: their/there/they're, your/you're, its/it's, then/than, lose/loose, to/too/two, accept/except. Wrong: 'Your welcome.' / 'better then'. Right: 'You're welcome.' / 'better than'.

lesson.whatItIs: Some English words sound the same or very similar but are spelled differently and mean different things. Spell-check won't catch them, because each one is a real word.

form.pattern: their (belongs to them) / there (place, existence) / they're (they are)
form.example: They're in their room over there.
You're right about your booking.

form.pattern: its (belongs to it) / it's (it is, it has)
form.example: It's late. The hotel closed its bar.
Check the log, then call. It's bigger than that.
Don't lose the key. The handle is loose.
I went to the desk. Me too. Two keys.
We accept cards. Everyone except Rafael.

examples: They're checking their bags over there.
You're welcome.
It's colder than yesterday.
First we eat, then the speeches start.

commonMistakes.wrong: Plan B is better then Plan A.
commonMistakes.right: Plan B is better than Plan A.

commonMistakes.wrong: I don't want to loose my job.
commonMistakes.right: I don't want to lose my job.

tips: Test contractions: if you can say 'it is', 'you are' or 'they are', use the apostrophe.
'Then' is about time; 'than' is about comparing.

title: Other / another / others / the other
explanation: another + singular noun (one more / a different one); other + plural or uncountable noun; others = other ones (no noun); the other(s) = the remaining one(s). Wrong: 'another people', 'the others guests'. Right: 'other people', 'the other guests'.

lesson.whatItIs: These words talk about additional or different people and things. The right form depends on whether the noun is singular or plural, whether a noun follows, and whether you mean the remaining ones in a group.
whenToUse: Asking for one more or a different one: 'Can I have another towel?'
Talking about different people or things: 'Other guests complained too.'
Talking about the rest of a group: 'The other rooms are full.'

form.pattern: another + singular noun (one more / a different one)
form.example: Can I have another key?
Other guests were angry.
Some guests stayed; others left.

form.pattern: the other + singular (the second of two)
form.example: One ring was in the box; the other one was missing.

form.pattern: the other + plural / the others (the rest of a group)
form.example: The other guests are waiting. The others are waiting.
Rafael and Grace blamed each other.

examples: Could you give me another room?
Some people trusted Mateo; others didn't.
Hana is here. Where are the others?
Let's try another option.

commonMistakes.why: 'Another' is only used with a singular noun.

tips: 'Another' = an + other, so it is always followed by a singular noun (or a number: 'another two days').
Only 'others' (with no noun after it) takes -s.

title: Present tenses for the future
explanation: Use the present continuous for fixed personal arrangements and the present simple for timetables and schedules. Wrong: 'The plane will leave at 6 according to the timetable.' / 'I meet her tomorrow at 5.' (arranged) Right: 'The plane leaves at 6.' / 'I'm meeting her tomorrow at 5.'

lesson.whatItIs: English often uses present tenses to talk about the future. The present continuous shows a plan that is already arranged (with a time, a place or other people). The present simple shows an official timetable or schedule.
whenToUse: Personal arrangements: 'We're flying home on Friday.'
Timetables, schedules and programmes: 'The ceremony starts at 5:30.'

form.example: I'm meeting the caterer at 10.
The supply flight arrives at noon.
start, begin, leave, arrive, open, close, finish
I'm going to call her. — OK, I'll call her now.

examples: The plane leaves in 40 minutes.
We're moving the ceremony to the boathouse tomorrow.
What time does the reception finish?
Are you working tonight?

commonMistakes.wrong: The train will leave at 8 according to the timetable.

commonMistakes.why: 'What do you do?' asks about your job.

commonMistakes.wrong: The shop is opening at 9 every day.
commonMistakes.right: The shop opens at 9 every day.

tips: Always add a future time word so the meaning is clear: tonight, tomorrow, on Friday.
If you've already booked or agreed it, use the present continuous.

title: Present perfect
explanation: have/has + past participle for experiences, recent results and unfinished time. Wrong: 'I lose my key.' (result now) Right: 'I've lost my key.'

lesson.whatItIs: The present perfect connects the past to now. Use it for life experiences, past actions that have a result now, and situations that started in the past and are still continuing.
whenToUse: Experience with no time given: 'Have you ever been to Italy?'
A past action with a result now: 'I've lost my key (so I can't get in).'
Unfinished time: 'I've worked here for two days.'
Recent news with just / already / yet: 'The plane has just landed.'

form.example: I have lost my key.
She's left.
He hasn't called.

form.pattern: Question: Have / Has + subject + past participle?
form.example: Have you seen the rings?
seen, taken, found, been, gone, done

examples: Someone has taken 200 euros.
Have you finished the summary yet?
I've already called the technician.
She's never seen snow.

commonMistakes.why: A past action with a present result → present perfect.
Use the past participle, not the past simple.
'Went' is past simple; 'gone' is the participle.

tips: 'been' vs 'gone': 'She's been to Rome' (she came back) vs 'She's gone to Rome' (she is there now).
'yet' in negatives and questions; 'already' in positive sentences.

title: Present perfect vs past simple
explanation: Use past simple with a finished time (yesterday, at 3 PM); present perfect with no specific time. Wrong: 'I have seen him yesterday.' Right: 'I saw him yesterday.'

lesson.whatItIs: Both talk about the past. Use the past simple for finished actions at a specific, finished time. Use the present perfect when no time is given, or when the time period isn't finished yet.
whenToUse: Choosing the right tense for something in the past

form.example: yesterday, last week, at 3 PM, in 2020, two days ago

form.pattern: Present perfect + no time or unfinished time
form.example: ever, never, just, already, yet, today, this week, so far
When did you see him?

form.pattern: News: present perfect first, details in past simple
form.example: I've lost my bag. I lost it at the airport.

examples: I've lost my bag. I lost it at the airport this morning.
Have you ever met Luca? — Yes, I met him last year.
The storm has lasted three days. (it's still going)
The storm lasted three days. (it's over)

commonMistakes.why: 'When' asks for a specific time → past simple.

commonMistakes.wrong: Did you ever go to Lisbon?
commonMistakes.right: Have you ever been to Lisbon?

commonMistakes.why: Started in the past and still true → present perfect.

tips: If you can answer 'when?' with a finished time, use the past simple.
With managers: 'I've checked the log' (result) → 'I checked it at 2 AM' (detail).

title: For vs since
explanation: for + a period (for two hours), since + a starting point (since 9 AM). Wrong: 'I've waited since two hours.' Right: 'I've waited for two hours.'

lesson.whatItIs: For and since say how long something has continued up to now. Use 'for' with a period of time and 'since' with the starting point. Both usually go with the present perfect.
whenToUse: Talking about duration up to now

form.example: for two hours, for three days, for years
since 9 AM, since Monday, since 2020, since I arrived
How long have you worked here?

form.pattern: Present perfect continuous for an ongoing activity
form.example: I've been waiting for an hour.

examples: We've been stuck here since Tuesday.
I've known Daniel for ten years.
She's been in bed since this morning.
How long have you been waiting?

commonMistakes.wrong: How long are you working here?
commonMistakes.right: How long have you been working here?
commonMistakes.why: Duration up to now → present perfect (continuous).

tips: Can you count it (two hours)? → for. Is it a point on the clock or calendar? → since.
'Ago' is different and uses the past simple: 'I arrived two days ago.'

title: Must / have to / should
explanation: must/have to for obligation, should for advice, don't have to = not necessary, mustn't = not allowed. Wrong: 'You don't have to go outside alone.' (meaning forbidden) Right: 'You mustn't go outside alone.'

lesson.whatItIs: Must and have to express obligation, should gives advice, and the negatives have different meanings: mustn't = not allowed; don't have to = not necessary.

form.example: You must sign in.
I have to work tonight.
You should rest.
You mustn't go out alone.

form.pattern: don't have to + base verb (not necessary)
form.example: You don't have to pay.
I had to stay.

examples: All staff must report bear sightings.
We have to leave in 40 minutes.
You should tell Amara the truth.
You don't have to come, but you can.

commonMistakes.wrong: You don't have to go out alone. (meaning: forbidden)
commonMistakes.why: mustn't = forbidden; don't have to = optional.

tips: 'Should' is softer, which makes it good for advising guests and colleagues.
'Need to' works like 'have to': 'I need to check.'

title: Might / may / could for possibility
explanation: might/may/could + base verb for uncertain possibilities. Wrong: 'Maybe it can be in the laundry.' Right: 'It might be in the laundry.'

lesson.whatItIs: Might, may and could say that something is possible but not certain. They are followed by the base verb. Use can't when something is impossible and must when you are almost sure.

form.example: It might be in the laundry.
He may not come.
It can't be Grace — she was upstairs.
You must be tired.
He might be lying.

examples: The storm could last a week.
Rafael might know something.
It may rain at six.
That can't be true.

commonMistakes.wrong: Maybe it can be in the laundry.
commonMistakes.right: It might be in the laundry.
commonMistakes.why: 'Can' isn't used for this kind of guess.

commonMistakes.wrong: It could not be him. (meaning: impossible)

tips: Certainty scale: must (sure) > may / might / could (possible) > can't (impossible).
'Maybe' is an adverb: 'Maybe it's there' = 'It might be there'.

title: First conditional
explanation: If + present simple, will + verb, for real future possibilities. Wrong: 'If the storm will come, we will move inside.' Right: 'If the storm comes, we'll move inside.'

lesson.whatItIs: The first conditional talks about real, possible future situations and their results. The if-clause uses the present simple, even though it refers to the future.

form.pattern: If + present simple, will + base verb
form.example: If the storm comes, we'll move inside.
We'll move inside if the storm comes.
Unless you tell her, I will.
If you see a bear, call me.

examples: If Luca agrees, we'll have both dishes.
If you don't hurry, we'll miss the window.
I'll call you if I find it.
If it rains, use Plan A.

commonMistakes.wrong: If the storm will come, we will move.
commonMistakes.right: If the storm comes, we will move.

commonMistakes.wrong: If you will see him, tell me.
commonMistakes.right: If you see him, tell me.

tips: 'when' works the same way for things that will surely happen: 'When I arrive, I'll call you.'
Use a comma only when the if-clause comes first.

title: Second conditional
explanation: If + past simple, would + verb, for unreal or unlikely situations. Wrong: 'If I would be you, I will tell her.' Right: 'If I were you, I'd tell her.'

lesson.whatItIs: The second conditional talks about unreal, imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future. The past tense in the if-clause doesn't mean past time: it means 'not real'.

form.pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb
form.example: If I had more fuel, I'd run the freezer.
If I were you, I'd tell her.
If we left earlier, we could avoid the storm.

form.pattern: Question: What would you do if...?
form.example: What would you do if you found the rings?

examples: If I were the manager, I would fire him.
What would you do if you found the rings?
If the villa had more space, everyone would fit.
I wouldn't do that if I were you.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I would be you, I will tell her.
commonMistakes.right: If I were you, I'd tell her.
commonMistakes.why: No 'would' in the if-clause; 'would' in the result.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I have money, I would buy it. (unreal)
commonMistakes.right: If I had money, I would buy it.

tips: First = realistic, second = imaginary: 'If I win' (I might) vs 'If I won' (I probably won't).
'If I were you, I'd...' is the most useful advice phrase in English.

title: Gerund vs infinitive
explanation: Some verbs take -ing (enjoy, avoid, suggest, mind), others take to + verb (want, decide, agree, refuse). Wrong: 'I suggest to move inside.' Right: 'I suggest moving inside.'

lesson.whatItIs: When one verb follows another, the second verb is either a gerund (-ing) or an infinitive (to + verb). It depends on the first verb, so learn the common patterns.

form.pattern: verb + -ing: enjoy, avoid, suggest, mind, finish, keep, deny, risk
form.example: I suggest moving inside.

form.pattern: verb + to + verb: want, decide, agree, refuse, promise, plan, need, hope, offer, manage
form.example: She refused to cook it.
interested in working, before leaving, thank you for helping

form.pattern: Different meaning: stop, remember, forget, try
form.example: I stopped smoking (quit) / I stopped to smoke (in order to)

examples: Rafael denied taking the money.
Luca agreed to cook jollof.
Would you mind waiting?
I remember locking the drawer.
tips: After any preposition, always use -ing.
To express purpose, use 'to': 'I came to help.'

title: Relative clauses (who / which / that / where)
explanation: who for people, which for things, where for places; don't repeat the pronoun. Wrong: 'The man which called...', 'The bag that I lost it.' Right: 'The man who called...', 'The bag that I lost.'

lesson.whatItIs: Relative clauses give more information about a noun using who, which, that, where or whose. They let you combine two short sentences into one.
whenToUse: Identifying which person or thing you mean

form.example: The guest who complained is in room 214.
The watch, which was gold, was in the laundry.

form.pattern: that (people or things, defining clauses only)
form.example: The bag that I lost was black.
the room where it happened
the woman whose watch was lost

form.pattern: Defining (no commas) vs non-defining (commas, extra info, no 'that')
form.example: Lisbon, which is beautiful, ...

examples: The concierge who booked the taxi is Rafael.
The file that you uploaded was changed.
Mrs. Tanaka, who is 78, travels alone.
That's the boathouse where we'll hold the ceremony.

commonMistakes.wrong: The bag that I lost it.

commonMistakes.why: No 'that' in a clause with commas.

commonMistakes.wrong: the guest who his watch was lost
commonMistakes.right: the guest whose watch was lost

tips: You can drop who/that/which when it is the object: 'the bag (that) I lost'.
Use 'where' only for places.

title: Passive voice
explanation: be + past participle when the action matters more than who did it. Wrong: 'The watch was find in the laundry.' Right: 'The watch was found in the laundry.'

lesson.whatItIs: The passive focuses on the action or the thing affected, not on who did it. Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant. Form it with 'be' + past participle.
whenToUse: Official and formal language: 'Your booking has been cancelled.'

form.example: Rooms are cleaned daily.
The watch was found.

form.pattern: Present perfect: has / have been + past participle
form.example: The flight has been cancelled.

form.pattern: Future / modal: will be / must be + past participle
form.example: The guests must be informed.
The rings were found by Funmilayo.

examples: 200 euros were taken from the drawer.
The data was changed at 3:20.
Breakfast is served from 7.
The ceremony will be moved indoors.

commonMistakes.why: The flight didn't cancel itself; you need 'been'.

tips: The passive can avoid blame politely: 'Mistakes were made.'
Verbs without objects (happen, arrive, die) have no passive form.

title: Reported speech
explanation: Usually move tenses back and change pronouns. Wrong: 'She said she is leaving tomorrow.' (when it's later) Right: 'She said she was leaving the next day.'

lesson.whatItIs: Reported speech tells what someone said without quoting their exact words. Usually the tense moves one step back, and pronouns and time words change.

form.example: is → was, will → would, can → could, did / has done → had done
She said (that)... / She told me (that)...

form.pattern: Yes/no questions: asked if / whether + statement order
form.example: He asked if I had a receipt.
She asked where the rings were.

form.pattern: Commands: told / asked + person + to + verb
form.example: Inês told me to count the cash.
today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there

examples: Mr. Weller said he had been travelling for 14 hours.
Rafael told me the driver was his friend.
Kofi asked me which file I had uploaded.
Astrid told us not to go out alone.

commonMistakes.wrong: She said me she was tired.
commonMistakes.right: She told me she was tired. / She said she was tired.

commonMistakes.wrong: He asked where was the key.
commonMistakes.right: He asked where the key was.

commonMistakes.wrong: She said she is leaving tomorrow. (said last week)
commonMistakes.right: She said she was leaving the next day.
commonMistakes.why: Move the tense and the time word back.

tips: If something is still true now, you can keep the tense: 'He said he likes jollof.'
Very useful for reporting to managers.

title: Used to / be used to
explanation: used to + verb = past habit; be used to + -ing = accustomed to. Wrong: 'I am used to work at night.' Right: 'I'm used to working at night.'

lesson.whatItIs: Used to + verb describes past habits or states that are no longer true. Be used to + -ing means being familiar or comfortable with something. Get used to + -ing means becoming familiar with it.
whenToUse: Talking about adapting to something new

form.example: I used to work days.
He didn't use to smoke.

form.pattern: Question: Did you use to + verb?
form.example: Did you use to live here?
I'm used to working nights.
You'll get used to the cold.

examples: Mateo used to be honest.
I'm not used to the darkness.
She's getting used to her new job.
We used to have a bigger generator.

commonMistakes.wrong: I am used to work at night.
commonMistakes.right: I'm used to working at night.

commonMistakes.wrong: I use to live in Rome.
commonMistakes.right: I used to live in Rome.

commonMistakes.wrong: I used to go there yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: A single past event → past simple.

tips: used to = no longer true; usually = still true now.
'would' can also describe repeated past actions: 'Every summer we would go to the lake.'

title: Phrasal verbs
explanation: Verb + particle with a special meaning (look into, figure out, call off). Wrong: 'We will look the problem.' Right: 'We will look into the problem.'

lesson.whatItIs: Phrasal verbs are a verb + a particle (up, out, off, into...) with a meaning that is often different from the verb alone. They are very common in everyday spoken English.
whenToUse: Everyday speech, chat and informal messages
Formal writing often uses a single verb instead (investigate, cancel)

form.example: give up, show up, run out

form.pattern: Separable: object can go in the middle
form.example: turn the light off / turn it off

form.pattern: Pronoun objects must go in the middle
form.example: turn it off (not 'turn off it')
look into the problem, look after the guests
run out of fuel, put up with noise
look into = investigate, figure out = understand, call off = cancel, find out = discover, sort out = fix

examples: We'll look into the problem.
We're running out of fuel.
I found out the truth.
They called off the outdoor ceremony.

commonMistakes.right: We will look into the problem.
commonMistakes.why: Without the particle the meaning changes.
A pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.

commonMistakes.right: I will find out the truth.

tips: Learn phrasal verbs in a sentence, not as a list.
With managers, a single verb often sounds more formal: investigate, cancel, continue.

title: Verb / adjective + preposition
explanation: Many words need a fixed preposition (depend on, apologise for, interested in, responsible for). Wrong: 'I apologise about the delay.' Right: 'I apologise for the delay.'

lesson.whatItIs: Many verbs, adjectives and nouns are followed by a fixed preposition. There is often no logical rule, so learn the word and its preposition together.

form.example: apologise for, depend on, listen to, wait for, belong to, complain about, pay for
interested in, responsible for, afraid of, good at, married to, worried about
reason for, solution to, problem with, increase in
responsible for checking

examples: I apologise for the delay.
Who is responsible for the cash drawer?
It depends on the weather.
Is there a solution to this?
tips: Write them down with a full example sentence.
Some verbs take no preposition: discuss (not 'discuss about'), contact, enter.

title: Run-ons and sentence fragments
explanation: A sentence needs a subject and a verb; join two full sentences with a linker or a full stop, not just a comma. Wrong: 'The lift stopped, I called the technician.' Right: 'The lift stopped, so I called the technician.'

lesson.whatItIs: A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and must express a complete idea. Two complete sentences can't be joined with only a comma (a run-on), and a group of words without a subject or verb is a fragment.

form.example: The lift stopped.
The lift stopped, so I called the technician.

form.pattern: Or separate with a full stop
form.example: The lift stopped. I called the technician.
The lift stopped; I called the technician.

form.pattern: Fix a fragment: attach it or add a subject and verb
form.example: Because the taxi was slow. → I was late because the taxi was slow.

examples: Mr. Weller arrived at 11:40, but his room was gone.
Hana fell. Her ankle is swollen.
Although it was dark, we found him.
We need fuel because the plane isn't coming.

commonMistakes.wrong: The lift stopped, I called the technician.
commonMistakes.right: The lift stopped, so I called the technician.
commonMistakes.why: A comma alone can't join two sentences.

commonMistakes.right: I left because I was tired.
commonMistakes.why: This is a fragment; it needs a main clause.

commonMistakes.right: He was very angry about the taxi.

commonMistakes.wrong: I checked the log it was empty.
commonMistakes.right: I checked the log. It was empty.
commonMistakes.why: Two sentences need a full stop or a linker.

tips: In reports, short clear sentences are better than long ones.
Read each sentence alone: does it make sense by itself?

title: Present perfect continuous
explanation: have/has been + -ing for an activity that started in the past and is still continuing, or has just stopped with a visible result. Wrong: 'I am waiting here for two hours.' Right: 'I've been waiting here for two hours.'

lesson.whatItIs: The present perfect continuous focuses on an activity and how long it has lasted, from the past until now. It can also explain a present result of a recent activity.
whenToUse: How long, up to now: 'I've been waiting for an hour.'
A recent activity with a result now: 'You look tired. Have you been working all night?'

form.example: I've been looking for it.
He hasn't been sleeping well.
How long have you been waiting?
She's been working here since June.

examples: We've been running the generator for 20 hours.
Mateo has been changing the data for months.
Why are you wet? — I've been checking the mast.
How long have you been working here?

commonMistakes.wrong: I am waiting here for two hours.
commonMistakes.right: I've been waiting here for two hours.
commonMistakes.why: Duration up to now → present perfect continuous.

commonMistakes.wrong: I've been knowing him for years.
commonMistakes.why: State verbs use the present perfect simple.

commonMistakes.wrong: She has been writing three emails.
commonMistakes.why: A finished number of things → present perfect simple.

commonMistakes.wrong: How long you have been waiting?
commonMistakes.right: How long have you been waiting?

tips: Continuous = the activity or how long; simple = the result or how many: 'I've been writing all day. I've written five reports.'
Very natural with 'all day', 'all night', 'lately', 'recently'.

title: Question tags (isn't it? / did you?)
explanation: Add a short tag to check information or invite agreement: positive sentence → negative tag, negative sentence → positive tag, using the same auxiliary. Wrong: 'You are the manager, isn't it?' Right: 'You're the manager, aren't you?'

lesson.whatItIs: Question tags are short questions at the end of a sentence. We use them to check that something is true or to invite agreement. The tag uses the same auxiliary verb and subject as the sentence, in the opposite form.

form.example: It's late, isn't it?
You didn't see it, did you?

form.pattern: Use the auxiliary from the sentence
form.example: She can swim, can't she?
He works here, doesn't he?
I'm right, aren't I? / Let's go, shall we? / Nobody called, did they?

examples: You were at the desk at 2 AM, weren't you?
The plane hasn't left yet, has it?
Rafael booked the taxi, didn't he?
We can't move the date, can we?

commonMistakes.wrong: You are the manager, isn't it?
commonMistakes.why: Use the same verb and subject: are you → aren't you.
The tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I'.

tips: Falling intonation = you expect agreement; rising intonation = you're really asking.
In chat, 'right?' is an informal tag: 'You were there, right?'

title: Quantifiers (few / a few / little / a little / plenty of)
explanation: a few (countable) / a little (uncountable) = some (positive); few / little = almost none (negative). Wrong: 'We have little guests.' / 'I have few money.' Right: 'We have a few guests.' / 'I have a little money.'

lesson.whatItIs: Quantifiers tell you how much or how many. 'A few' and 'a little' sound positive (some, enough), while 'few' and 'little' without 'a' sound negative (not enough).

form.example: We have a few rooms left.
Few guests complained.
There's a little fuel left.
There's little hope.

form.pattern: a lot of / lots of (both types)
form.example: a lot of guests, a lot of fuel
We have plenty of food.

examples: Give me a few minutes.
We have very little time.
Only a few people knew the truth.
There's plenty of coffee.
tips: 'Only a few' and 'very little' make it clear the amount is small.
In speech, use 'a lot of' in positive sentences; 'much' and 'many' sound formal there.

title: Both / either / neither
