explanation: both = the two (plural verb); either = one or the other; neither = not one and not the other (singular verb, positive form). Wrong: 'Neither of them don't know.' Right: 'Neither of them knows.'

lesson.whatItIs: These words talk about two things or people. 'Both' means the two together; 'either' means one of the two (it doesn't matter which); 'neither' means not one and not the other.

form.pattern: both + plural / both A and B
form.example: Both options are risky. Both Hana and Mateo are outside.

form.pattern: either + singular / either A or B
form.example: Either plan works. Either we move inside or we start earlier.

form.pattern: neither + singular / neither A nor B
form.example: Neither answer is correct. Neither Rafael nor Grace saw it.

form.pattern: both / either / neither of + the / them / us
form.example: Neither of them called.
Neither do I. / Either is fine.

examples: Both plans have problems.
You can choose either option.
Neither Kofi nor Astrid agreed.
Neither of the stories is true.

commonMistakes.why: 'Neither' is already negative; use a positive verb.

commonMistakes.right: Both plans / Both of the plans

commonMistakes.wrong: Either Grace or Rafael are lying.
commonMistakes.right: Either Grace or Rafael is lying.
commonMistakes.why: With either / or, the verb matches the nearest noun.

commonMistakes.wrong: Both Hana and Mateo is outside.
commonMistakes.right: Both Hana and Mateo are outside.

tips: 'Either' in negatives = 'any of the two': 'I don't like either option.'
'Neither of them are' is common in speech, but 'is' is correct in writing.

title: So / such
explanation: so + adjective/adverb; such + (a/an) + adjective + noun; both can be followed by 'that' + result. Wrong: 'It was so a long night.' / 'I'm such tired.' Right: 'It was such a long night.' / 'I'm so tired.'

lesson.whatItIs: 'So' and 'such' make adjectives stronger, like 'very', and can introduce a result with 'that'. The grammar after each one is different.
whenToUse: Explaining a result: 'It was so cold that the pipes froze.'

form.example: so cold, so quickly

form.pattern: such + a / an + adjective + singular noun
form.example: such a long night
such nice people, such bad weather
so many guests, so much luggage
She was so angry that she left.

examples: It was such a strange night.
The storm was so strong that the flight was cancelled.
There were so many guests!
Thank you, you've been so helpful.

commonMistakes.wrong: It was so a long night.
commonMistakes.right: It was such a long night.

commonMistakes.wrong: It was a so good idea.
commonMistakes.right: It was such a good idea.

tips: 'Such' needs a noun; 'so' doesn't.
In speech, 'that' is often dropped: 'I was so tired I fell asleep.'

title: So do I / Neither do I
explanation: Agree with a positive statement using So + auxiliary + subject, and with a negative one using Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject. Wrong: 'I'm tired. — So I am.' / 'I don't know. — Neither I do.' Right: 'So am I.' / 'Neither do I.'

lesson.whatItIs: These short replies show that the same is true for you or someone else. They use the auxiliary from the first sentence, with inverted word order.
whenToUse: Saying that the same is true for another person

form.example: 'I'm cold.' — 'So am I.'
'I can't sleep.' — 'Neither can I.'
'I loved the food.' — 'So did I.'
Me too. / Me neither.
'I'm tired.' — 'I'm not.' / 'I didn't see it.' — 'I did.'

examples: 'I didn't see the bear.' — 'Neither did Mateo.'
'Hana wants to leave.' — 'So does Astrid.'
'We've never been here.' — 'Neither have we.'
'I can help.' — 'So can I.'

commonMistakes.why: Invert: the auxiliary comes before the subject.

tips: 'Me too' and 'Me neither' are fine in chat.
Copy the auxiliary: am → am, can → can, has → has; no auxiliary → do / does / did.

title: Future time clauses (when / before / after / until / as soon as)
explanation: After when, before, after, until and as soon as, use the present (not will) to talk about the future. Wrong: 'I'll call you when I will arrive.' Right: 'I'll call you when I arrive.'

lesson.whatItIs: When a time clause talks about the future, the verb inside it is in the present tense. 'Will' goes only in the main clause.
whenToUse: Plans and promises about the future

form.pattern: Main clause (will / imperative) + time word + present simple
form.example: I'll call you when I arrive.

form.pattern: Time words: when, before, after, until, as soon as, once
form.example: Don't move until I say so.

form.pattern: Present perfect for a completed action
form.example: I'll tell you as soon as I've finished.
As soon as the storm stops, we'll leave.

examples: Call me as soon as you're inside.
We'll serve dinner after the speeches finish.
I won't leave until the technician arrives.
Before you go out, check the radio.

commonMistakes.wrong: I'll call you when I will arrive.
commonMistakes.right: I'll call you when I arrive.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wait until I will tell you.
As soon as she will finish, we go.
commonMistakes.right: As soon as she finishes, we'll go.
commonMistakes.why: Present in the time clause, 'will' in the main clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: After I will check, I tell you.
commonMistakes.right: After I check, I'll tell you.

tips: It works like the first conditional: no 'will' after if or when.
'until' = up to that time; 'by' = no later than: 'by 6 PM'.

title: Make / let / allow (someone do something)
explanation: make + person + base verb (force); let + person + base verb (permit); allow + person + to + verb. Wrong: 'He made me to wait.' / 'Let me to explain.' / 'They allowed me go.' Right: 'He made me wait.' / 'Let me explain.' / 'They allowed me to go.'

lesson.whatItIs: These verbs talk about forcing or permitting someone to do something. 'Make' and 'let' are followed by the base verb with no 'to'; 'allow' needs 'to'.
whenToUse: Explaining pressure: 'He made me sign it.'

form.example: Inês made me count the cash again.
Let me explain.
Guests are allowed to smoke outside.

form.pattern: Passive: be made to + verb / be allowed to + verb
form.example: I was made to wait. We're not allowed to go out.

form.pattern: 'Let' has no passive → be allowed to
form.example: We weren't allowed to leave.

examples: Astrid won't let anyone go out alone.
The storm made us cancel the flight.
Let me check that for you.
Staff aren't allowed to take cash home.
tips: 'Let me...' is a polite offer: 'Let me call a taxi for you.'
'Let's' (let us) = a suggestion; 'let me' = an offer.

title: Verb + object + to-infinitive (want someone to...)
explanation: Verbs like want, ask, tell, expect, need and advise + person + to + verb. Wrong: 'I want that you call me.' / 'She told me wait.' Right: 'I want you to call me.' / 'She told me to wait.'

lesson.whatItIs: Many verbs that express wishes, requests and orders use the pattern verb + person + to + verb. Many languages use 'that' + clause here, but English usually doesn't.

form.pattern: want / would like + person + to + verb
form.example: I want you to call me.

form.pattern: ask / tell / remind + person + to + verb
form.example: Astrid told us to stay inside.

form.pattern: advise / encourage / persuade + person + to + verb
form.example: I persuaded Mateo to tell the truth.
We need you to sign here.
She told me not to worry.

examples: Mrs. Tanaka asked me to find the watch.
I'd like you to check the log.
Chiara expects us to be ready by noon.
Remind me to call the villa.

commonMistakes.wrong: I want that you call me.
commonMistakes.right: I want you to call me.

commonMistakes.wrong: He asked to me to help.

commonMistakes.right: I don't want you to go.

tips: 'Suggest' and 'recommend' are different: 'I suggest that you rest' or 'I suggest resting', never 'suggest you to'.
'Let' and 'make' don't use 'to' (see make / let / allow).

title: -ed vs -ing adjectives (bored / boring)
explanation: -ed adjectives describe how people feel; -ing adjectives describe the thing or person that causes the feeling. Wrong: 'I am boring.' (meaning I feel bored) Right: 'I am bored. The meeting is boring.'

lesson.whatItIs: Many adjectives have two forms. The -ed form describes a feeling someone has. The -ing form describes what causes that feeling.

form.example: I'm tired. She's worried. We were shocked.
The night was tiring. The news is worrying. It was shocking.
bored/boring, interested/interesting, confused/confusing, surprised/surprising, embarrassed/embarrassing, exhausted/exhausting

examples: Mrs. Tanaka was very confused.
The situation is confusing.
I'm exhausted after this shift.
It was an embarrassing speech.

commonMistakes.wrong: I am boring. (meaning: I feel bored)
I'm very exciting about the trip.
commonMistakes.right: I'm very excited about the trip.

tips: People can be -ing too: 'He's boring' means other people feel bored because of him.
Ask: is this the feeling (-ed) or the cause (-ing)?

title: Each / every / all
explanation: each/every + singular noun + singular verb; all + plural or uncountable noun. Wrong: 'Every guests have a key.' Right: 'Every guest has a key.'

lesson.whatItIs: All three talk about a whole group, but the grammar and focus differ. 'Each' looks at members one by one; 'every' sees the whole group but uses a singular noun; 'all' uses a plural noun.
whenToUse: Rules and procedures: 'Each room has a safe.'

form.example: Each guest gets a key.
Every room has a safe.
All guests must check out by 11. All the fuel is gone.

form.pattern: each of / all of + the / them
form.example: Each of them has a radio. All of us were tired.
every day, every 30 minutes

examples: Each incident has three milestones.
Every member of staff must sign in.
All the guests were safe.
Check in every 30 minutes.

commonMistakes.right: Each of them / All of them

tips: Use 'each' for two things: 'She had a ring on each hand.'
'Everyone' and 'everybody' are singular: 'Everyone is here.'

title: Had better / would rather
explanation: had better + base verb = strong advice or warning; would rather + base verb = preference. Wrong: 'You had better to go.' / 'I would rather to stay.' Right: 'You'd better go.' / 'I'd rather stay.'

lesson.whatItIs: 'Had better' gives strong advice or a warning about now or the near future (despite 'had', it isn't past). 'Would rather' expresses what you prefer.

form.example: You'd better hurry.
We'd better not tell her yet.
I'd rather stay inside.
I'd rather move indoors than risk the storm.
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.

examples: You'd better call Inês now.
We'd better leave before the window closes.
I'd rather not discuss it.
Amara would rather have a smaller ceremony than get wet.

commonMistakes.why: For another person's action, use the past simple.

tips: 'Had better' sounds urgent or even a little threatening; use 'should' for gentle advice.
'I'd prefer to' means the same as 'I'd rather' and is more formal.

title: Tense consistency
explanation: Keep the same time frame throughout a story or message; change tense only when the time really changes. Wrong: 'I went to the desk and I see Rafael.' Right: 'I went to the desk and I saw Rafael.'

lesson.whatItIs: When you tell a story or write a report, choose a time frame and keep it. Switching between past and present for no reason confuses the reader.

form.pattern: Story in the past: keep past forms
form.example: The lift stopped, so I called Grace.

form.pattern: Change tense only when the time really changes
form.example: Last night the lift stopped. It's working now.
I realised someone had taken the money.

form.pattern: Reports: past for events, present for the current state
form.example: The guest complained at 1 AM. He is waiting for a reply.

examples: At 2 AM the power went out and Tobias got stuck in the lift.
I checked the drawer, but the money was gone.
Mrs. Tanaka lost her watch last night. It's safe now.
When I arrived, everyone was waiting.

commonMistakes.wrong: I went to the desk and I see Rafael.
commonMistakes.right: I went to the desk and I saw Rafael.
commonMistakes.why: Keep the story in the past.

commonMistakes.wrong: Yesterday he says he was outside.
commonMistakes.right: Yesterday he said he was outside.

commonMistakes.wrong: She called me and tells me the news.
commonMistakes.right: She called me and told me the news.
commonMistakes.why: Same time frame for both actions.

commonMistakes.wrong: The lift stops at 2 AM and I called Grace.
commonMistakes.right: The lift stopped at 2 AM and I called Grace.

tips: Before sending a report, check every verb: is it in the same time frame?
Some people tell funny stories in the present for drama, but keep reports in the past.

title: Adverbs of degree (quite / rather / fairly / pretty / extremely)
explanation: Adverbs of degree make adjectives stronger or weaker; their strength and position matter. Wrong: 'It's a quite good idea.' / 'very perfect'. Right: 'It's quite a good idea.' / 'perfect' (or 'absolutely perfect').

lesson.whatItIs: Adverbs of degree tell you how much. Some make an adjective stronger (very, extremely, really), some make it weaker (fairly, a bit, slightly), and 'quite' and 'rather' change meaning depending on context.
whenToUse: Softening criticism: 'The price is a bit high.'

form.example: It's extremely cold.
The boathouse is quite small.

form.pattern: Weak: fairly, a bit, slightly, a little
form.example: The invoice is slightly higher than agreed.

form.pattern: quite / rather + a / an + adjective + noun
form.example: It was quite a long night. It's rather an odd story.

form.pattern: a bit / a little + negative adjectives (not positive)
form.example: a bit late, a bit expensive (not 'a bit beautiful')

examples: The storm is extremely dangerous.
Mateo seemed pretty relaxed.
The price is a bit high for us.
It was rather a strange speech.

commonMistakes.why: Strong adjectives don't take 'very' (see strong adjectives).
'A bit' is used with negative or neutral adjectives.
'Too much' is used with nouns, not adjectives.

tips: In British English, 'quite good' often means 'okay, not great'; tone of voice matters.
'A bit' softens complaints politely: 'The room is a bit cold.'

title: Compound adjectives (a ten-minute walk / a two-hour delay)
explanation: In compound adjectives before a noun, use a hyphen and a singular noun: number + singular noun. Wrong: 'a ten-minutes walk', 'a 5 stars hotel'. Right: 'a ten-minute walk', 'a five-star hotel'.

lesson.whatItIs: A compound adjective is two or more words joined by a hyphen that together describe a noun. When a number is part of it, the noun stays singular, because it is acting like an adjective (and adjectives have no plural in English).
whenToUse: Describing time, distance, age, size and price
Describing people and things: 'a well-known caterer'

form.example: a ten-minute walk, a two-hour delay, a 400-kilo limit
a 78-year-old woman
a well-known chef, a last-minute change
a hand-written log, a world-famous villa

form.pattern: After the noun: no hyphen, normal plural
form.example: The walk takes ten minutes. She is 78 years old.

examples: We have a 40-minute weather window.
Mrs. Tanaka is a 78-year-old widow.
It was a last-minute decision.
He stayed in a five-star hotel.

commonMistakes.why: Before a noun, the noun in the compound stays singular.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is a 78 years old woman.

commonMistakes.why: After the noun, use the normal form.

tips: Test: if it comes before a noun, make it singular with hyphens.
Compound adjectives make reports shorter: 'a delay of two hours' → 'a two-hour delay'.

title: 'It' as an empty subject (It's important to... / It takes... / It's raining)
explanation: English sentences need a subject, so 'it' is used for weather, time, distance and to introduce an idea that comes later. Wrong: 'Is important to call.' / 'Is raining.' Right: 'It's important to call.' / 'It's raining.'

lesson.whatItIs: In English, every sentence needs a subject, even when there is no real 'doer'. 'It' fills this empty position. Many languages can leave the subject out, so learners often forget this 'it'.
whenToUse: Time, dates and distance: 'It's 2 AM.' 'It's 400 metres.'
Introducing an idea: 'It's important to stay calm.'

form.example: It's cold. It's late. It's far.
It's important to report it.
It's clear that he lied.
It takes me ten minutes to walk there.
It seems that the file was changed.

examples: It's dangerous to go out alone.
It took two hours to fix the lift.
It's obvious that Sophie hid the rings.
It's getting dark.

commonMistakes.right: It takes two hours to fix.

commonMistakes.wrong: To go out alone is dangerous. (possible but very formal)
commonMistakes.right: It's dangerous to go out alone.
commonMistakes.why: English prefers 'it' first and the long idea at the end.

tips: English likes to put long ideas at the end of the sentence, with 'it' at the start.
Don't confuse 'it is' with 'there is': 'There's a problem' (exists) / 'It's a problem' (describes).

title: Past ability (could / was able to / managed to)
explanation: could = general past ability; was able to / managed to = success on one specific occasion; couldn't works for both. Wrong: 'The lift stopped, but I could open it.' Right: 'The lift stopped, but I managed to open it.'

lesson.whatItIs: For general ability in the past, use 'could'. For one specific situation where someone succeeded, English uses 'was able to' or 'managed to', not 'could'. In the negative, 'couldn't' works in both cases.
whenToUse: General ability: 'I could swim when I was five.'
One specific success: 'We managed to land before the storm.'

form.example: Grace could speak four languages.

form.pattern: was / were able to + verb (specific success)
form.example: Kofi was able to restart the generator.
We managed to calm him down.

form.pattern: couldn't / wasn't able to / didn't manage to (failure)
form.example: I couldn't reach Inês.

form.pattern: could with senses and mental verbs is fine for one occasion
form.example: I could see the bear on the camera.

examples: I managed to find the watch in the laundry.
Elif was able to land despite the wind.
When she was young, Funmilayo could cook for 200 people.
We couldn't open the lift door.

commonMistakes.wrong: The lift stopped, but I could open it.
commonMistakes.right: The lift stopped, but I managed to open it.
commonMistakes.why: One specific success → managed to / was able to.

commonMistakes.wrong: We could catch the last flight yesterday.
commonMistakes.right: We were able to catch the last flight yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: A specific achievement → was / were able to.

tips: 'Managed to' suggests it was difficult, which is great for reports: 'I managed to calm the guest.'
The negative is easy: 'couldn't' is always fine.

title: Just / yet / still / already
explanation: just = very recently; already = sooner than expected; yet = up to now (negatives and questions, at the end); still = continuing longer than expected. Wrong: 'I didn't finish yet.' / 'I already have finished.' Right: 'I haven't finished yet.' / 'I've already finished.'

lesson.whatItIs: These four adverbs are often used with the present perfect to talk about time up to now. Each one has a fixed meaning and a fixed position in the sentence.

form.pattern: just: between have / has and the participle (very recently)
form.example: The plane has just landed.

form.pattern: already: between have / has and the participle (earlier than expected)
form.example: I've already called the technician.

form.pattern: yet: end of negatives and questions (up to now)
form.example: Has Kofi fixed it yet? He hasn't finished yet.

form.pattern: still: before the main verb, or before haven't / hasn't (continuing)
form.example: She still hasn't replied. We're still waiting.

form.pattern: American English often uses the past simple with these
form.example: I already called him. (US)

examples: Inês has just arrived.
I've already checked the log twice.
Have the guests arrived yet?
Rafael still hasn't explained where he was.

commonMistakes.why: With 'yet', British English uses the present perfect.

commonMistakes.right: I have already finished. / I haven't finished yet.
commonMistakes.why: 'Yet' is for negatives and questions, at the end.

tips: Status reports use these a lot: 'The lift is fixed. The cash is still missing. Inês hasn't replied yet.'
'Not yet' alone is a complete answer: 'Has he called? — Not yet.'

title: Past perfect
explanation: had + past participle for an action before another past action. Wrong: 'When I arrived, the plane already left.' Right: 'When I arrived, the plane had already left.'

lesson.whatItIs: The past perfect describes an action that happened before another action in the past. It makes the order of past events clear.

form.example: The plane had left.
I hadn't seen it.
Had you met him before?
When I arrived, the plane had already left.

form.pattern: Time words: already, before, by the time, after, just
form.example: By the time she called, I had finished.

examples: By the time Inês arrived, Rafael had changed his story.
I realised I had left the drawer open.
She had never seen a polar bear before.
After they had eaten, the speeches began.

commonMistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the plane already left.
commonMistakes.right: When I arrived, the plane had already left.

commonMistakes.wrong: I had seen him yesterday. (single event)
commonMistakes.why: Use the past perfect only to order two past events.

commonMistakes.wrong: Before she arrived, I have finished.
commonMistakes.right: Before she arrived, I had finished.
commonMistakes.why: Earlier than a past event → had + participle.

tips: If 'before' or 'after' already shows the order, the past simple is also fine.
Great for alibis and reports: 'By 2 AM I had already checked the doors.'

title: Third conditional
explanation: If + past perfect, would have + past participle, for imagined past results. Wrong: 'If I would have known, I would tell you.' Right: 'If I had known, I would have told you.'

lesson.whatItIs: The third conditional imagines a different past and its result. It is used for regrets, criticism and explaining what could have happened.

form.pattern: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle
form.example: If I had known, I would have told you.
If we had left earlier, we might have avoided the storm.
If you hadn't called, he would have panicked.
I'd have, I wouldn't have (spoken: would've)

examples: If Grace hadn't kept a log, we wouldn't have caught him.
If I had checked the list, this wouldn't have happened.
What would you have done if the bear had come closer?
She would have cried if she'd seen the speech.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would tell you.
commonMistakes.right: If I had known, I would have told you.
commonMistakes.why: 'had' + participle after 'if'; 'would have' + participle in the result.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I knew yesterday, I would come.
commonMistakes.right: If I had known yesterday, I would have come.

tips: 'I'd' can mean 'I had' or 'I would': 'If I'd known, I'd have come.'
Formal inversion has the same meaning: 'Had I known, I would have come.'

title: Modals of deduction (must / can't / might have)
explanation: must have / can't have / might have + past participle for conclusions about the past. Wrong: 'He must took it.' Right: 'He must have taken it.'

lesson.whatItIs: Modals of deduction show how sure you are about something, based on evidence. For the present, use modal + verb. For the past, use modal + have + past participle.

form.pattern: Present: must be (sure), might / could be (possible), can't be (impossible)
form.example: He must be tired.
He must have taken it.

form.pattern: Past (possible): might / could have + past participle
form.example: She might have forgotten.

form.pattern: Past (impossible): can't / couldn't have + past participle
form.example: It can't have been Grace.
He must have been lying.

examples: Rafael must have taken the money — only he had the key.
The rings can't have disappeared by themselves.
Mateo might have changed the file while we were busy.
You must be exhausted.

commonMistakes.why: The opposite of 'must' for deduction is 'can't'.

tips: 'should have' + participle is different: it means criticism or regret ('You should have told me').
Use these forms to make polite, evidence-based accusations.

title: Wish and regret
explanation: wish + past simple for present regrets, wish + past perfect for past regrets. Wrong: 'I wish I know the answer.' Right: 'I wish I knew the answer.'

lesson.whatItIs: 'Wish' expresses that you want a situation to be different. The tense after 'wish' moves back: past for present wishes, past perfect for past regrets, and 'would' for wanting someone else to change.

form.example: I wish I knew the answer.
I wish I hadn't said that.
I wish Daniel would decide.
If only I had checked the list!
I regret trusting him.

examples: I wish we had more fuel.
Mateo wishes he hadn't changed the data.
I wish you would stop joking.
If only the storm had come later.

commonMistakes.wrong: I wish I know the answer.
commonMistakes.right: I wish I knew the answer.

commonMistakes.wrong: I wish I didn't say that. (past)
commonMistakes.right: I wish I hadn't said that.

commonMistakes.wrong: I wish I would be taller.

tips: 'I wish I were' is formal; 'I wish I was' is common in speech.
For future hopes, use 'hope', not 'wish': 'I hope you feel better.'

title: Causative (have / get something done)
explanation: have/get + object + past participle when someone else does the job. Wrong: 'I will repair my ankle checked.' Right: 'I'll have my ankle checked.'

lesson.whatItIs: The causative (have / get something done) shows that someone else does a job for you. The focus is on the result, not on who does it.

form.example: I'll have my ankle checked.
We need to get the generator fixed.
She had her dress altered.

form.pattern: have + person + base verb (ask someone to do it)
form.example: I'll have Grace check the room.
I'll get Kofi to fix it.

examples: We had the lift repaired at 4 AM.
Could you have the speech printed?
I'll get the rings cleaned.
Inês had Rafael's locker searched.

commonMistakes.wrong: I will repair my ankle checked.
I cut my hair. (a barber did it)
We need to get fixed the generator.
commonMistakes.right: We need to get the generator fixed.
commonMistakes.why: The object comes before the participle.

tips: It is also used for bad experiences: 'He had his bag stolen.'
Very useful for delegating politely at work.

title: Contrast linkers (although / despite / however)
explanation: although + clause, despite + noun or -ing, however between sentences. Wrong: 'Despite it was raining, we started.' Right: 'Although it was raining, we started.' / 'Despite the rain, we started.'

lesson.whatItIs: Contrast linkers show that two ideas are different or surprising. Each linker needs specific grammar after it: a clause, a noun, or a new sentence.

form.example: Although it was raining, we started.

form.pattern: despite / in spite of + noun or -ing
form.example: Despite the rain, we started. / Despite being tired, she stayed.
It was raining. However, we started.
Plan A is safe, whereas Plan B is beautiful.
It was raining, but we started.

examples: Although Luca was angry, he agreed.
Despite the storm, the plane landed.
The boathouse is small. However, it is dry.
In spite of the evidence, he denied it.

commonMistakes.wrong: Despite it was raining, we started.
commonMistakes.right: Although it was raining, we started.
commonMistakes.why: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing, not a clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: Although it rained, but we went.
However it was late we continued.
commonMistakes.right: It was late. However, we continued.
commonMistakes.why: 'However' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma.

commonMistakes.right: Despite the rain / In spite of the rain

tips: 'Despite the fact that' + clause also works.
'Even though' is stronger than 'although'.

title: Indirect questions
explanation: After 'Could you tell me...' use statement word order. Wrong: 'Could you tell me where is the lift?' Right: 'Could you tell me where the lift is?'

lesson.whatItIs: Indirect questions are polite questions that start with a phrase like 'Could you tell me...' or 'Do you know...'. After the phrase, use normal statement word order with no do / does / did.
whenToUse: Polite questions to guests, clients, managers and strangers

form.pattern: Could you tell me + wh-word + subject + verb?
form.example: Could you tell me where the lift is?

form.pattern: Do you know if / whether + subject + verb?
form.example: Do you know if he has a receipt?
I was wondering when the plane leaves.

form.pattern: No do / does / did after the opening phrase
form.example: Do you know what time it starts?

examples: Could you tell me what happened?
Do you know where Rafael was at 2 AM?
I'd like to know why the invoice is higher.
Can you remember when you last saw it?

commonMistakes.wrong: Could you tell me where is the lift?
commonMistakes.right: Could you tell me where the lift is?

commonMistakes.wrong: Do you know what time does it start?
commonMistakes.right: Do you know what time it starts?

commonMistakes.wrong: Can you tell me did he call?
commonMistakes.right: Can you tell me if he called?

commonMistakes.wrong: I wonder where are the rings.
commonMistakes.right: I wonder where the rings are.

tips: Use a question mark only if the whole sentence is a question: 'I wonder where it is.' ends with a full stop.
Indirect questions sound more polite than direct ones.

title: Formal vs informal register
explanation: Match tone to the situation: formal with managers and clients, casual with friends. Wrong (to a manager): 'Hey, the cash thing is messed up lol.' Right: 'I'm afraid there is a problem with the cash drawer.'

lesson.whatItIs: Register is the level of formality. The same message changes depending on who you are talking to: friends (informal), colleagues (neutral), managers, clients and official messages (formal).

form.pattern: Formal: full forms, polite modals, no slang or emojis
form.example: I am afraid that..., Could you please...
I'm afraid..., Unfortunately..., I would appreciate it if...
get → receive, help → assist, need → require, tell → inform, ask for → request

form.pattern: Informal: contractions, slang, emojis, phrasal verbs
form.example: Hey, can u sort it out? 👍

examples: Informal: 'Hey, the cash thing is messed up lol.' → Formal: 'I'm afraid there is a discrepancy in the cash drawer.'
Informal: 'Can u send it?' → Formal: 'Could you please send it?'
Informal: 'Sorry, my bad.' → Formal: 'I apologise for the error.'

commonMistakes.wrong: Hey Inês, the money is gone lol
commonMistakes.right: Inês, I'm afraid 200 euros are missing from the drawer.

commonMistakes.wrong: Dear Sir, wanna confirm the booking?
commonMistakes.right: Dear Sir, I would like to confirm your booking.
commonMistakes.why: Mixed register: formal greeting with slang.

commonMistakes.right: Could you please provide a receipt?
commonMistakes.why: Too direct for a formal situation.

commonMistakes.wrong: I want that you call me.
commonMistakes.right: I would appreciate it if you could call me.

tips: Ask yourself: would I say this to my boss? If not, rewrite it.
Being too formal with friends sounds cold. Match the person.

title: Future continuous and future perfect
explanation: will be + -ing = an action in progress at a future time; will have + past participle = completed before a future time. Wrong: 'By 6 PM I will finish.' Right: 'By 6 PM I will have finished.'

lesson.whatItIs: The future continuous describes something in progress at a specific moment in the future. The future perfect describes something that will be completed before a certain future time.
whenToUse: Future continuous: 'This time tomorrow we'll be flying home.'
Polite questions about plans: 'Will you be staying long?'

form.example: At 5:30 we'll be holding the ceremony.
By noon, Kofi will have fixed the generator.
by Friday, by the time you arrive

form.pattern: Negative: won't be + -ing / won't have + past participle
form.example: We won't have finished by 6.

examples: This time tomorrow, Hana will be resting in hospital.
By the time the plane lands, we'll have packed everything.
Will you be needing a taxi?
In ten years, the glacier will have disappeared.

commonMistakes.right: By 6 PM I will have finished.
At 8 tomorrow I will be working.
commonMistakes.why: In progress at a future moment → future continuous.

commonMistakes.wrong: By the time you will arrive, ...

tips: 'Will you be + -ing?' is a polite way to ask about someone's plans.
'By' is the key signal for the future perfect.

title: Impersonal passive (It is said that... / He is believed to...)
explanation: Report general opinions formally with It + passive + that-clause, or subject + passive + to-infinitive. Wrong: 'He is believed that he took it.' Right: 'It is believed that he took it.' / 'He is believed to have taken it.'

lesson.whatItIs: This structure reports what people in general say, think or believe, without saying who. It is common in news, reports and formal writing.

form.pattern: It + is said / believed / thought / reported + that + clause
form.example: It is believed that the data was changed.

form.pattern: Subject + is said / believed + to + verb (present)
form.example: He is said to be very honest.

form.pattern: Subject + is believed + to have + past participle (past)
form.example: He is believed to have taken the money.
say, believe, think, report, expect, know, consider

examples: The storm is expected to hit at six.
It is reported that 200 euros went missing.
Luca is said to be the best caterer on the lake.
The scientist is thought to have falsified the results.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is believed that he took it.
commonMistakes.right: It is believed that he took it. / He is believed to have taken it.

commonMistakes.wrong: It is said he to be rich.
commonMistakes.right: He is said to be rich.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is thought to take it yesterday.
commonMistakes.right: He is thought to have taken it yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: A past action → to have + past participle.

tips: It is useful for hedging: it shows the information isn't confirmed.
Use it in formal reports, not in casual chat.

title: Participle clauses (Hearing the alarm, ... / Having finished, ...)
explanation: -ing, past participle and having + past participle clauses can replace a full clause, but their subject must be the same as the main clause. Wrong: 'Walking to the mast, the bear appeared.' Right: 'Walking to the mast, we saw a bear.'

lesson.whatItIs: Participle clauses make writing shorter and more formal by replacing a full clause with a participle. The hidden subject of the participle must be the same as the subject of the main clause.

form.example: Hearing the alarm, Grace ran downstairs.
Having checked the log, I called Inês.
Shocked by the news, Amara sat down.
Before leaving, check the radio. While waiting, I read the report.
The man standing at the desk is Tobias.

examples: Having finished the count, Inês noticed the problem.
Built in 1890, the villa has no lift.
Feeling nervous, Daniel told a joke.
The guests waiting in the lobby were angry.

commonMistakes.wrong: Walking to the mast, the bear appeared.
commonMistakes.right: Walking to the mast, we saw a bear.
commonMistakes.why: The participle's subject must be the main subject.

commonMistakes.wrong: Finished the report, I sent it.
commonMistakes.right: Having finished the report, I sent it.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'having' for an earlier active action.

commonMistakes.right: As it was raining, we stayed in.
commonMistakes.why: Different subject → use a full clause.

tips: Check: who is doing the -ing? It must be the subject after the comma.
Use these in writing; in speech, full clauses sound more natural.

title: Should have / could have / would have
explanation: should have + past participle = criticism or regret; could have + past participle = possible but didn't happen; would have + past participle = imagined result or willingness. Wrong: 'You should told me.' / 'I should of called.' Right: 'You should have told me.' / 'I should have called.'

lesson.whatItIs: Modal + have + past participle talks about the past in an unreal way: what was a good idea but didn't happen, what was possible, or what someone was willing to do.
whenToUse: Criticism and regret: 'You should have called.'
Missed possibilities: 'We could have avoided this.'
Willingness: 'I would have helped, but nobody asked.'

form.pattern: should have + past participle (right, but it didn't happen)
form.example: You should have told me.

form.pattern: shouldn't have + past participle (it happened, but it was wrong)
form.example: I shouldn't have trusted him.

form.pattern: could have + past participle (possible but didn't happen)
form.example: Someone could have been hurt.

form.pattern: would have + past participle (imagined result / willingness)
form.example: I would have called, but my phone died.
Never write 'should of'.

examples: I should have checked the guest list myself.
Mateo shouldn't have changed the data.
The bear could have attacked them.
I would have called you, but the line was down.

commonMistakes.why: 'Of' is a mistake for the sound of 've.

tips: Soften criticism: 'Maybe it would have been better to...'
'Must have' (deduction) is different from 'should have' (criticism).

title: Be supposed to
explanation: be supposed to + verb = what is expected, planned or required (in the past, often something that didn't happen). Wrong: 'The plane supposed to land at 6.' Right: 'The plane was supposed to land at 6.'

lesson.whatItIs: 'Be supposed to' talks about what is expected because of a rule, plan or arrangement. In the past, it often means the expected thing didn't happen.
whenToUse: Rules: 'You're not supposed to go out alone.'
Plans that failed: 'The flight was supposed to arrive today.'
What people say: 'It's supposed to rain.'

form.pattern: am / is / are supposed to + verb
form.example: You're supposed to sign in.

form.pattern: was / were supposed to + verb (it didn't happen)
form.example: The supply plane was supposed to come today.
Staff aren't supposed to take cash home.
What am I supposed to do?

examples: The ceremony was supposed to start at 5:30.
You're not supposed to open the safe without a manager.
Sophie was supposed to send the right list.
It's supposed to be the best restaurant on the lake.

commonMistakes.wrong: The plane supposed to land at 6.
commonMistakes.right: The plane was supposed to land at 6.

commonMistakes.why: Base verb after 'to'; put 'be' in the past.

tips: 'What am I supposed to do?' can express frustration or ask for instructions.
It is softer than 'must' and good for explaining rules.

title: Unless / as long as / provided that / in case
explanation: unless = if not; as long as / provided (that) = only if; in case = as a precaution. Wrong: 'Unless you don't hurry, we'll miss it.' / 'Take the radio if case you need it.' Right: 'Unless you hurry, we'll miss it.' / 'Take the radio in case you need it.'

lesson.whatItIs: These words replace 'if' to add a specific meaning: an exception, a condition that must be met, or a precaution.

form.example: We'll go unless it rains.

form.pattern: as long as / so long as (= only if)
form.example: You can go out as long as someone goes with you.
Luca will cook it provided that he has help.
Take a rifle in case you see a bear.
Hurry, otherwise we'll miss the window.

examples: We won't move the ceremony unless the forecast gets worse.
You can leave early as long as the handover is done.
Provided the price is fair, we'll sign.
Keep the torch in case the power goes again.

commonMistakes.wrong: Unless you don't hurry, we'll miss it.
commonMistakes.right: Unless you hurry, we'll miss it.

commonMistakes.wrong: Take the radio if case you need it.
commonMistakes.right: Take the radio in case you need it.

commonMistakes.wrong: In case it will rain, take an umbrella.
commonMistakes.right: In case it rains, take an umbrella.

commonMistakes.wrong: As long as you will help, ...

tips: 'In case' is not 'if': 'Take an umbrella in case it rains' means take it now, as a precaution.
Great for negotiation: 'We can accept that, provided that...'

title: Purpose linkers (so that / in order to / so as to)
explanation: in order to / so as to + verb; so that + subject + can/could/will/would. Wrong: 'I left early so that to avoid traffic.' Right: 'I left early in order to avoid traffic.' / 'I left early so that I could avoid traffic.'

lesson.whatItIs: Purpose linkers explain why something is done. 'In order to' and 'so as to' are followed by a verb. 'So that' is followed by a full clause, usually with a modal verb.

form.pattern: to / in order to / so as to + base verb
form.example: We cut the heating in order to save fuel.

form.pattern: Negative: in order not to / so as not to + verb
form.example: Speak quietly so as not to scare it.

form.pattern: so that + subject + can / will (present / future)
form.example: I'll write it down so that I won't forget.
She hid the rings so that the wedding would fail.

examples: We moved the ceremony earlier so that guests would stay dry.
I'm calling in order to confirm the numbers.
Walk slowly so as not to slip.
Kofi checked the tank so that we could plan.

commonMistakes.wrong: I left early so that to avoid traffic.
commonMistakes.right: I left early to avoid traffic.

commonMistakes.wrong: In order to not slip, walk slowly.
commonMistakes.right: In order not to slip, walk slowly.

commonMistakes.wrong: She hid them so that the wedding fails.
commonMistakes.right: She hid them so that the wedding would fail.

tips: Use 'so that' when the subject changes: 'I explained it so that she would understand.'
'In order to' sounds formal; in chat, just use 'to'.

title: Cause and result linkers (due to / since / therefore / as a result)
explanation: due to / because of / owing to + noun; as / since + clause; therefore / as a result / consequently start a result sentence. Wrong: 'Due to it was raining, we stayed.' Right: 'Due to the rain, we stayed.' / 'It rained. Therefore, we stayed.'

lesson.whatItIs: These linkers show cause and effect in more formal or precise ways than 'because' and 'so'. Each one needs specific grammar after it.

form.pattern: because of / due to / owing to + noun
form.example: The flight was cancelled due to the storm.
As the plane is late, we'll wait.

form.pattern: therefore / as a result / consequently (new sentence + comma)
form.example: Fuel was low. Therefore, we cut the heating.
The lift is broken, which means we'll use the stairs.
Fuel was low, so we cut the heating.

examples: Due to a system error, your booking was cancelled.
Since you were at the desk, you must have seen him.
The data was false. As a result, the funding was at risk.
Owing to the weather, the ceremony was moved indoors.

commonMistakes.wrong: Due to it was raining, we stayed.
commonMistakes.right: Due to the rain, we stayed. / Because it was raining, we stayed.
commonMistakes.why: 'Due to' is followed by a noun only.
'Therefore' normally starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon).

commonMistakes.wrong: Because of the plane is late...
As a result of we had no fuel
commonMistakes.right: As a result of the fuel shortage

tips: In reports, 'due to' sounds professional: 'The delay was due to a power cut.'
Don't use 'therefore' in casual chat; 'so' is more natural.

title: Addition linkers (moreover / furthermore / in addition / as well as)
explanation: Add points formally with moreover, furthermore, in addition (new sentence + comma); in addition to / as well as / besides + noun or -ing. Wrong: 'In addition to check the log, I called.' Right: 'In addition to checking the log, I called.'

lesson.whatItIs: Addition linkers add another point to an argument. They are more formal than 'and' or 'also', and some are followed by nouns or -ing forms.
whenToUse: Building a case: 'Moreover, his story changed twice.'

form.pattern: Moreover / Furthermore / In addition, + clause (new sentence)
form.example: His alibi is weak. Moreover, Grace's log contradicts it.

form.pattern: in addition to / as well as / besides + noun or -ing
form.example: In addition to the fee, he charged 150 per guest.
He not only lied but also blamed me.
It's cold. What's more, the fuel is low.

examples: The boathouse is dry. Furthermore, it's close to the villa.
As well as fixing the lift, Kofi checked the generator.
Besides being late, the invoice was wrong.
Rafael booked the taxi. In addition, he had the drawer key.

commonMistakes.wrong: In addition to check the log, I called.
commonMistakes.right: In addition to checking the log, I called.

commonMistakes.why: Put a comma after the linker.

commonMistakes.wrong: As well as he fixed the lift...
commonMistakes.right: As well as fixing the lift...

tips: Use one or two per paragraph; too many sound robotic.
'Besides' at the start of a sentence = 'anyway, another reason': 'Besides, it's too late now.'

title: Advanced comparisons (the more..., the more / far better / twice as)
explanation: Modify comparatives with much/far/slightly; use the + comparative, the + comparative for things that change together; comparative + and + comparative for continuous change. Wrong: 'The more you wait, more expensive it gets.' Right: 'The longer you wait, the more expensive it gets.'

lesson.whatItIs: Beyond simple comparisons, English uses special structures to show how big a difference is, how two things change together, and how something keeps changing.

form.pattern: much / far / a lot / slightly / a bit + comparative
form.example: far safer, slightly cheaper
The longer we wait, the worse it gets.
It's getting colder and colder.

form.pattern: not nearly as / nowhere near as... as
form.example: It's not nearly as bad as I thought.
The invoice is twice as high as agreed.

examples: The sooner we decide, the better.
The storm is getting worse and worse.
Plan B is far riskier than Plan A.
Luca's price is nowhere near as fair as he says.

commonMistakes.wrong: The more you wait, more expensive it gets.
commonMistakes.right: The longer you wait, the more expensive it gets.

commonMistakes.why: Use much / far, not very, with comparatives.

tips: 'The sooner, the better' is a useful fixed phrase.
'Far' and 'much' make differences bigger; 'slightly' and 'a bit' make them smaller.

title: Reporting verbs (deny, admit, suggest, insist, warn, accuse...)
explanation: Reporting verbs follow fixed patterns: deny/admit/suggest + -ing; agree/refuse/promise + to-verb; warn/advise/remind + person + to-verb; insist on + -ing; accuse someone of + -ing. Wrong: 'He denied to take it.' / 'She suggested me to rest.' Right: 'He denied taking it.' / 'She suggested that I rest.'

lesson.whatItIs: Instead of always using 'said', you can use reporting verbs that show the speaker's intention (deny, admit, warn, insist). Each verb has its own grammar pattern.

form.example: He denied taking the money.

form.pattern: verb + to + verb: agree, refuse, promise, offer, threaten
form.example: Luca refused to cook jollof.

form.pattern: verb + person + to + verb: warn, advise, remind, persuade, encourage
form.example: Astrid warned us not to go out.

form.pattern: verb + preposition + -ing: insist on, apologise for, accuse someone of, blame someone for
form.example: Rafael accused me of leaving the drawer open.

form.pattern: suggest / recommend + that + subject + base verb
form.example: I suggested that she rest.

examples: Mateo admitted changing the data.
Funmilayo insisted on serving jollof rice.
Kofi reminded me to check the tank.
Sophie apologised for causing trouble.

commonMistakes.right: She suggested that I rest. / She suggested resting.

tips: Reporting verbs make reports shorter: 'He said it wasn't him' → 'He denied it.'
Learn each verb with its pattern in one example sentence.

title: Unreal past (it's time / would rather / as if)
explanation: After 'it's time', 'would rather' (+ another person), 'as if' / 'as though' and 'suppose', a past tense can describe an unreal present or future. Wrong: 'It's time we leave.' / 'I'd rather you don't tell her.' Right: 'It's time we left.' / 'I'd rather you didn't tell her.'

lesson.whatItIs: In some expressions, English uses a past tense to talk about the present or future when the situation is unreal, imagined or hasn't happened yet, just like after 'wish' and in the second conditional.
whenToUse: Saying something should already be happening: 'It's time we left.'
Preferences about other people's actions: 'I'd rather you stayed.'
Imagined comparisons: 'He talks as if he owned the place.'

form.pattern: It's (high / about) time + subject + past simple
form.example: It's time we moved inside.
It's time to go.
I'd rather you didn't tell her yet.
He acts as if he were innocent.
Suppose the plane didn't come. What would we do?

examples: It's high time Mateo told the truth.
I'd rather you called me before deciding.
Luca speaks as if he were doing us a favour.
Imagine we lost all our power. What would we do?

commonMistakes.why: After 'it's time + subject', use the past.

commonMistakes.wrong: I'd rather you don't tell anyone.
commonMistakes.right: I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
commonMistakes.why: Use the past for another person's action.

commonMistakes.wrong: He acts as if he is the boss. (he isn't)
commonMistakes.right: He acts as if he were the boss.

commonMistakes.wrong: It's high time to we go.
commonMistakes.right: It's high time we went. / It's time to go.

tips: 'As if' + present is fine when something might be true: 'It looks as if it's going to rain.'
'It's high time' adds criticism: it should have happened already.

title: Past perfect continuous
explanation: had been + -ing for an activity that continued up to a point in the past, often explaining a past result. Wrong: 'I was waiting for two hours when he arrived.' Right: 'I had been waiting for two hours when he arrived.'

lesson.whatItIs: The past perfect continuous describes an activity that had been happening for some time before another moment in the past. It focuses on duration, or on the cause of a past situation.
whenToUse: Duration up to a past moment: 'We'd been working for 20 hours when the generator failed.'
Explaining a past result: 'Her eyes were red because she had been crying.'

form.example: I had been waiting for an hour.
He hadn't been sleeping well.
How long had you been working there?
She'd been looking for the watch since dinner.

examples: Hana had been working outside for an hour when the bear appeared.
Mateo had been changing the data for months before Kofi noticed.
The guests were angry because they had been waiting since noon.
How long had you been standing there?

commonMistakes.wrong: I was waiting for two hours when he arrived.
commonMistakes.right: I had been waiting for two hours when he arrived.
commonMistakes.why: Duration before a past moment → past perfect continuous.

commonMistakes.wrong: She had been knowing him for years.
commonMistakes.right: She had known him for years.
commonMistakes.why: State verbs use the past perfect simple.

commonMistakes.wrong: He had been wrote three emails.
commonMistakes.why: A finished number → past perfect simple.

commonMistakes.wrong: I have been waiting when he came.
commonMistakes.right: I had been waiting when he came.

tips: It is the past version of the present perfect continuous: 'I've been waiting' → 'I had been waiting'.
Very useful for explaining causes in reports: 'The pipes burst because the heating had been off.'

title: Future in the past (was going to / would)
explanation: Use was/were going to, was/were about to and would to talk about the future from a point in the past, often for plans that didn't happen. Wrong: 'I am going to call you yesterday, but...' Right: 'I was going to call you yesterday, but...'

lesson.whatItIs: Sometimes we talk about something that was in the future at a past moment. English uses past forms of future structures for this. It is often used for plans that changed or didn't happen.
whenToUse: Plans that didn't happen: 'We were going to marry outside, but it rained.'
Past predictions: 'I knew it would be a long night.'
Reported speech: 'She said she would help.'

form.pattern: was / were going to + verb (past plan or intention)
form.example: I was going to tell you.

form.pattern: would + verb (future seen from the past)
form.example: I thought the plane would arrive on time.

form.pattern: was / were about to + verb (very near)
form.example: I was about to call when you arrived.
We were leaving the next day.

examples: I was going to call you, but my battery died.
Nobody knew the storm would last a week.
Hana was about to finish when the bear appeared.
Luca said he would cook jollof.

commonMistakes.wrong: I am going to call you yesterday, but...
commonMistakes.right: I was going to call you yesterday, but...
commonMistakes.why: A past plan → was going to.

commonMistakes.wrong: We were going to married outside.
commonMistakes.right: We were going to marry outside.
commonMistakes.why: Use the base verb after 'going to'.

tips: 'I was going to..., but...' is the most natural way to explain a changed plan.
Polite excuse: 'I was going to ask you the same thing.'

title: Be about to / be due to / be to
explanation: be about to + verb = very soon; be due to + verb = scheduled; be to + verb = formal arrangement or instruction. Wrong: 'The plane is about to leaving.' / 'The report is due to finish tomorrow.' (meaning someone will finish it) Right: 'The plane is about to leave.' / 'The report is due tomorrow.'

lesson.whatItIs: These structures describe the future in specific ways: something that will happen in a moment, something that is planned or expected at a certain time, or a formal official arrangement.
whenToUse: Something will happen any second: 'The plane is about to take off.'
Schedules and deadlines: 'The flight is due to land at 3.'
Formal plans and instructions: 'All staff are to report at 7.'

form.pattern: be about to + base verb (very near future)
form.example: The ceremony is about to start.
The supply plane is due to arrive on Monday.
The invoice is due on Friday.
The inspector is to visit next week. You are not to leave the station.

form.pattern: Past: was about to / was due to
form.example: I was about to call you.

examples: Hurry, the window is about to close.
Elif's plane is due to land at noon.
The final payment is due after the event.
Guests are not to enter the kitchen.

commonMistakes.wrong: The plane is about to leaving.
commonMistakes.right: The plane is about to leave.
commonMistakes.why: Use the base verb after 'about to'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The ceremony is due to start soon at any second.
commonMistakes.right: The ceremony is about to start.

commonMistakes.wrong: The flight is due arriving at 3.
commonMistakes.right: The flight is due to arrive at 3.

commonMistakes.wrong: You are not leave the station.
commonMistakes.right: You are not to leave the station.

tips: Don't confuse 'due to' (scheduled) with 'due to' (because of): 'delayed due to the storm'.
'Be to' is common in news headlines and official rules.

title: Needn't have vs didn't need to
explanation: needn't have + past participle = you did it, but it wasn't necessary; didn't need to + verb = it wasn't necessary (and usually you didn't do it). Wrong: 'I needn't to bring it.' / 'I didn't need to brought it.' Right: 'I needn't have brought it.' / 'I didn't need to bring it.'

lesson.whatItIs: Both talk about something that wasn't necessary in the past, but they tell different stories. 'Needn't have done' means you did something unnecessary. 'Didn't need to do' simply says it wasn't necessary, and usually means you didn't do it.
whenToUse: Regretting an unnecessary action: 'I needn't have worried.'
Saying something wasn't required: 'We didn't need to pay.'

form.pattern: needn't have + past participle (did it, but it was unnecessary)
form.example: You needn't have called the police; we found the watch.

form.pattern: didn't need to + base verb (it wasn't necessary)
form.example: We didn't need to move inside; the storm passed.

form.pattern: Present: needn't + verb / don't need to + verb
form.example: You needn't wait. You don't need to wait.
We need to leave now.

examples: I needn't have panicked; the rings were in the bag.
We didn't need to cancel the ceremony after all.
You needn't have brought a gift.
Kofi didn't need to fix the generator; it restarted by itself.

commonMistakes.right: I needn't bring it. / I don't need to bring it.
commonMistakes.why: 'Needn't' is followed by the base verb, without 'to'.

commonMistakes.wrong: I didn't need to brought it.
commonMistakes.right: I didn't need to bring it.

tips: 'You needn't have!' is a polite reaction to a gift.
'Needn't' is mostly British; American English prefers 'didn't have to'.

title: Strong (non-gradable) adjectives (absolutely exhausted)
explanation: Strong adjectives (exhausted, freezing, furious, perfect) already mean 'very', so use absolutely/completely/totally, not very. Wrong: 'very exhausted', 'very freezing'. Right: 'absolutely exhausted', 'very tired'.

lesson.whatItIs: Normal (gradable) adjectives like tired, cold and angry can be made stronger with 'very'. Strong (non-gradable) adjectives like exhausted, freezing and furious already include the idea of 'very', so they use different adverbs.

form.pattern: very / extremely / a bit + normal adjective
form.example: very tired, extremely cold, a bit angry

form.pattern: absolutely / completely / totally / utterly + strong adjective
form.example: absolutely exhausted, completely freezing
really tired, really exhausted
tired → exhausted, cold → freezing, angry → furious, good → excellent, bad → terrible, big → huge, small → tiny, hungry → starving, scared → terrified

examples: I'm absolutely exhausted after this shift.
It's freezing outside.
Funmilayo was furious about the menu.
The food was absolutely delicious.

commonMistakes.why: 'Perfect' can't be more or less perfect.

tips: Strong adjectives make speaking more expressive: 'starving' sounds stronger than 'very hungry'.
'Quite' with strong adjectives means 'completely': 'You're quite right.'

title: Like vs as
explanation: as + role/job (= in the position of); like + noun (= similar to); as + clause / like + clause (informal). Wrong: 'She works like a nurse.' (her job) / 'As I, he hates the cold.' Right: 'She works as a nurse.' / 'Like me, he hates the cold.'

lesson.whatItIs: 'Like' and 'as' can both be translated in similar ways, but they mean different things. 'As' describes a real role or function. 'Like' compares two things that are similar.

form.pattern: as + role / job / function (it really is)
form.example: She works as a planner. Use the boathouse as a backup.
He talks like a lawyer. (he isn't one)
As I said, the price is fixed.
Nigerian dishes such as jollof rice

form.pattern: as if / as though (see unreal past)
form.example: He acts as if he owned the place.

examples: I'm working as the night receptionist.
Like Grace, I keep a log of everything.
As I mentioned, the storm arrives at six.
Mateo behaved like a friend until he was caught.

commonMistakes.wrong: She works like a nurse. (her job)
As I, he hates the cold.
commonMistakes.right: Like me, he hates the cold.
commonMistakes.why: Comparison with a noun / pronoun → like.

commonMistakes.wrong: He speaks as a native speaker. (he isn't one)
commonMistakes.right: He speaks like a native speaker.

commonMistakes.why: Before a clause in formal writing, use 'as'.

tips: Test: is it really that role? Yes → as. Only similar? → like.
'As usual' is a fixed phrase: 'Rafael was late, as usual.'

title: Negative questions (Didn't you see him? / Isn't it...?)
explanation: Negative questions show surprise, ask for confirmation or make suggestions; answer according to the facts (yes = it is true, no = it isn't). Wrong: 'Didn't you see him? — Yes, I didn't.' Right: 'No, I didn't.' / 'Yes, I did.'

lesson.whatItIs: Negative questions start with a negative auxiliary (Don't, Isn't, Didn't, Haven't). They can show surprise, check something you believe is true, criticise or suggest. Answering them confuses many learners: in English, you answer about the facts, not the question.
whenToUse: Checking something you think is true: 'Wasn't Rafael at the desk?'
Polite suggestions: 'Why don't we move inside?'

form.example: Didn't you lock the drawer?
Isn't the plane due at noon?
Why don't we ask Kofi?

form.pattern: Answer by the facts: Yes + positive / No + negative
form.example: 'Didn't you see it?' — 'No, I didn't.' (I didn't see it) / 'Yes, I did.' (I saw it)

form.pattern: Formal: Did you not...? / Is it not...?
form.example: Did you not receive our email?

examples: Didn't Grace check the laundry?
Isn't it a bit late to change the menu?
Why don't we start earlier?
Haven't you met Amara's mother?

commonMistakes.why: Answer by the facts: no + negative.
Yes always goes with a positive verb.
Use the negative of the modal.

tips: Ignore the 'not' in the question: decide the true fact, then say yes + positive or no + negative.
'Why don't we...?' is one of the friendliest ways to make a suggestion.

title: Degrees of certainty (definitely / likely to / bound to / chances are)
explanation: Show how sure you are with adverbs (definitely, probably) and phrases (be likely to, be bound to, there's a good chance); note the position: 'will probably' but 'probably won't'. Wrong: 'It will not probably rain.' / 'He is likely come.' Right: 'It probably won't rain.' / 'He is likely to come.'

lesson.whatItIs: English has many ways to say how certain you are, from 100% sure to very unlikely. Choosing the right one makes predictions, reports and negotiations precise.
whenToUse: Predictions: 'The storm will definitely reach us.'

form.example: The plane will definitely be late.
Luca will probably agree. He is likely to agree.
The storm might pass.
Mateo probably won't confess.
The rings definitely won't turn up by themselves.

form.pattern: be bound to / be sure to (almost certain)
form.example: Funmilayo is bound to notice.

form.pattern: There's a good chance (that) / Chances are (that)
form.example: Chances are the villa has a backup generator.

examples: The ceremony will probably start late.
Mateo is unlikely to admit it.
Someone is bound to ask about the missing money.
There's a good chance the storm will pass by six.
tips: Positive: will + probably / definitely. Negative: probably / definitely + won't.
'Likely' is an adjective, so you need 'be': 'It's likely to rain.'

title: Noun + noun, 's or of (a room key / the guest's bag / the end of the night)
explanation: Use noun + noun for types and common combinations (a hotel room), 's for people and animals (the guest's bag), and 'of' for things and parts (the end of the night); the first noun is usually singular. Wrong: 'a rooms key', 'the door of the manager', 'the night's end'. Right: 'a room key', 'the manager's door', 'the end of the night'.

lesson.whatItIs: English has three main ways to connect two nouns. The right one depends on whether the 'owner' is a person, a thing or a type.

form.example: a hotel room, a coffee cup, a gold watch

form.pattern: The first noun is usually singular
form.example: a room key (not 'a rooms key')
the guest's bag, Grace's logbook
the end of the night, the top of the mast
today's meeting, a week's holiday

form.pattern: a cup of tea (contents) vs a teacup (type)
form.example: Can I have a cup of coffee? Bring a coffee cup.

examples: The cash drawer was open.
Mrs. Tanaka's watch was in the laundry bag.
We met at the end of the shift.
Tonight's storm is the worst this year.

commonMistakes.why: The first noun is usually singular.

tips: Ask: is it a type (noun + noun), a person's ('s) or part of a thing (of)?
Too many nouns in a row are hard to read: 'hotel staff training session plan' → 'a plan for staff training'.

title: Mixed conditionals
explanation: Mix a past condition with a present result, or a present condition with a past result. Wrong: 'If I took that job, I would live in London now.' (the decision was in the past) Right: 'If I had taken that job, I would be living in London now.'

lesson.whatItIs: Mixed conditionals combine two different times: a past condition with a present result, or a present (permanent) condition with a past result.
whenToUse: How personality or permanent facts explain past events

form.pattern: Past condition → present result: If + had + participle, would + base verb
form.example: If I had taken that job, I would be living in London now.

form.pattern: Present condition → past result: If + past simple, would have + participle
form.example: If I were braver, I would have told her.
If he hadn't lied, we might trust him now.

examples: If Sophie hadn't hidden the rings, we wouldn't be in this mess now.
If Mateo were honest, he wouldn't have changed the data.
If I had brought my jacket, I wouldn't be cold.
If you didn't trust everyone, you would have noticed earlier.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I took that job, I would live in London now. (the decision was in the past)
commonMistakes.right: If I had taken that job, I would be living in London now.
commonMistakes.why: A past condition needs the past perfect.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I had been braver (in general), I would tell her yesterday.
commonMistakes.right: If I were braver, I would have told her yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: A permanent quality → past simple; a past result → would have.

commonMistakes.wrong: If he hadn't lied, he would have still been here now.
commonMistakes.right: If he hadn't lied, he would still be here now.
commonMistakes.why: A present result → would + base verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would be there.
commonMistakes.right: If I had known, I would be there.

tips: Decide the time of each half separately, then choose the form.
Words like 'now', 'today' and 'still' often signal a present result.

title: Inversion for emphasis
explanation: After negative adverbials (never, rarely, not only, no sooner) invert subject and auxiliary. Wrong: 'Never I have seen such a mess.' Right: 'Never have I seen such a mess.'

lesson.whatItIs: Inversion puts the auxiliary verb before the subject (like a question) after certain negative or limiting words at the start of a sentence. It adds emphasis and sounds formal or dramatic.

form.example: Never have I seen such a mess.
Not only did he lie, but he also blamed me.

form.pattern: No sooner + had + subject + participle + than
form.example: No sooner had we landed than the storm hit.
Hardly had I sat down when the alarm rang.

form.pattern: Only then / Only when + auxiliary + subject
form.example: Only then did I understand.
Had I known... / Should you need... / Were I you...

examples: Not only did Rafael take the money, but he also tried to blame you.
Rarely have we faced such a storm.
Should you need anything, please call.
Had we left earlier, we would have avoided it.

commonMistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such a mess.
commonMistakes.right: Never have I seen such a mess.
commonMistakes.why: The auxiliary goes before the subject.

commonMistakes.right: Not only did he lie, but...
commonMistakes.why: Add do / does / did with normal verbs.

commonMistakes.wrong: No sooner we had landed when...
commonMistakes.right: No sooner had we landed than...

tips: Don't overuse it in chat: it sounds very formal.
Perfect for speeches and formal reports.

title: Hedging and softening
explanation: Soften claims and criticism to sound diplomatic (it seems, perhaps, I'm not sure that...). Wrong (too blunt): 'You stole it.' Right: 'It seems your timeline doesn't quite match the log.'

lesson.whatItIs: Hedging means softening statements, opinions and criticism so you sound careful and diplomatic, not aggressive. It is essential in professional English, negotiations, and when you suspect something but have no full proof.

form.example: This could be a problem.

form.pattern: Softening verbs: seem, appear, tend to, suggest
form.example: It seems the file was changed.
I'm not sure..., I wonder if..., It's possible that...
Perhaps we could check again.
not entirely, a bit, Wouldn't it be better to...?

examples: It seems that your timeline doesn't quite match the log.
I'm not entirely sure this line is right for a wedding.
Perhaps we could look at the agreed price again?
There may have been a misunderstanding about the guest count.

commonMistakes.right: It appears the money went missing while you had the key.
I'm not sure some of these lines will land well with the guests.
I think there may be an error in the invoice.

commonMistakes.wrong: Maybe perhaps it could possibly be...

tips: Hedge your conclusion, not the facts: 'The file was changed at 3:20. It seems that...'
Use one hedge per point. Too many make you sound unsure.

title: Cleft sentences (It was... who / What I need is...)
explanation: Split a sentence to emphasise one part: It + be + focus + who/that..., or What + clause + be + focus. Wrong: 'It was Rafael which took it.' / 'What I need it is a receipt.' Right: 'It was Rafael who took it.' / 'What I need is a receipt.'

lesson.whatItIs: Cleft sentences split one idea into two parts to put focus on the most important information. They are common in both formal writing and emotional speech.
whenToUse: Correcting someone: 'It wasn't me who left the drawer open.'
Emphasising the key point: 'What worries me is the timeline.'

form.pattern: It + be + focus + who / that + rest
form.example: It was Grace who found the watch.
What I need is a clear timeline.
All I want is the truth.

form.pattern: The thing / reason / place + clause + be
form.example: The reason I called is the invoice.
What happened was that the generator failed.

examples: It was Sophie who sent the wrong list.
What surprised me was his calm.
It's not the money that matters, it's the trust.
All we can do now is wait.

commonMistakes.wrong: It was Rafael which took it.
commonMistakes.right: It was Rafael who took it.

commonMistakes.wrong: What I need it is a receipt.
commonMistakes.right: What I need is a receipt.

commonMistakes.wrong: It was at 2 AM when it happened.
commonMistakes.right: It was at 2 AM that it happened.
commonMistakes.why: After a time focus, use 'that' in careful writing.

commonMistakes.wrong: What happened is the lift stopped. (past story)
commonMistakes.right: What happened was that the lift stopped.
commonMistakes.why: Match the tense and add 'that' in formal writing.

tips: Use clefts to correct misunderstandings politely: 'It's the price, not the food, that we're discussing.'
Stress the focused word when speaking.

title: The subjunctive (I suggest that he be...)
explanation: After verbs and adjectives of demand or importance (suggest, insist, recommend, essential, vital), formal English uses the base verb for all subjects. Wrong (formal): 'I insist that he pays.' Right: 'I insist that he pay.' / 'It is essential that she be informed.'

lesson.whatItIs: The subjunctive is a formal form that uses the base verb (no -s, no past tense) after expressions of necessity, demand and recommendation. British English often uses 'should' + verb instead.
whenToUse: Formal writing, contracts and official recommendations

form.pattern: suggest / recommend / insist / demand / request + that + subject + base verb
form.example: The inspector recommended that she be promoted.

form.pattern: It is essential / vital / important / necessary + that + subject + base verb
form.example: It is vital that every guest be informed.

form.pattern: Negative: that + subject + not + base verb
form.example: We ask that guests not smoke inside.
I suggest that he should apologise.
if need be, be that as it may

examples: Astrid insisted that Mateo leave on the next flight.
It is essential that the manifest be accurate.
We recommend that the incident be reported.
The client requested that the invoice be corrected.

commonMistakes.why: The formal subjunctive uses the base verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: It's vital that she is told. (formal)
commonMistakes.right: It's vital that she be told.

commonMistakes.wrong: We ask that guests don't smoke.
commonMistakes.right: We ask that guests not smoke.

tips: In everyday British English, 'should' or the normal tense is acceptable; the subjunctive sounds very formal.
It is common in formal recommendations and official reports.

title: Ellipsis and substitution (I hope so / I'd love to / the black one)
explanation: Avoid repetition by leaving words out or replacing them with so, not, one(s), do so, a final auxiliary or a final 'to'. Wrong: 'I think yes.' / 'I hope no.' Right: 'I think so.' / 'I hope not.'

lesson.whatItIs: Natural English avoids repeating words that are already clear. Speakers leave words out (ellipsis) or use short substitute words (substitution). This makes speech sound fluent and natural.

form.pattern: think / hope / expect / guess + so / not
form.example: 'Will it rain?' — 'I hope not.'
He said he'd call, but he didn't.
'Can you come?' — 'I'd love to.'
'Which bag?' — 'The black one.'
Staff must report sightings and do so immediately.
Hana went out and slipped.

examples: 'Is the storm over?' — 'I don't think so.'
'Can you fix it?' — 'I'll try to.'
I wanted to tell her, but I couldn't.
These rings aren't the real ones.

commonMistakes.wrong: 'Do you want to come?' — 'I'd love to come to come.'

tips: 'I'm afraid so' / 'I'm afraid not' is a polite way to give bad news.
Short replies with auxiliaries sound more natural than repeating the whole sentence.

title: Nominalisation (formal noun phrases)
explanation: In formal writing, turn verbs and adjectives into nouns to sound objective and concise. Informal: 'Because the plane arrived late, we...' Formal: 'Due to the late arrival of the plane, we...'

lesson.whatItIs: Nominalisation means using a noun instead of a verb or adjective (decide → decision, arrive → arrival, important → importance). It makes writing more formal, concise and objective, which is why reports and academic writing use it a lot.
whenToUse: Reports, formal emails and academic writing

form.example: decide → decision, arrive → arrival, fail → failure, investigate → investigation
important → importance, available → availability, honest → honesty
because the generator failed → due to the failure of the generator
the cancellation of the flight
There has been an increase in... / We carried out an investigation.

examples: The cancellation of the supply flight caused a fuel shortage.
Following an investigation, the inspector made a recommendation.
The discovery of the rings led to a confrontation.
There was a significant increase in the invoice.

commonMistakes.wrong: Because Luca increased the price a lot, we complained. (formal report)
commonMistakes.right: Following a significant price increase, we filed a complaint.

commonMistakes.wrong: Due to the plane arrived late
commonMistakes.right: Due to the late arrival of the plane
commonMistakes.why: After 'due to', use a noun phrase.

commonMistakes.wrong: The investigation of the police investigated...
commonMistakes.why: Don't repeat the verb and noun.

tips: Don't overuse it: too many nouns make writing heavy. Use it in reports, not in chat.
Learn word families together: decide, decision, decisive, decisively.

title: Emphatic do (I do understand / I did lock it)
explanation: Add do/does/did before the base verb in a positive sentence to emphasise, contrast or insist. Wrong: 'I do understood.' / 'I did locked it.' Right: 'I did understand.' / 'I did lock it.'

lesson.whatItIs: In positive sentences, English can add 'do', 'does' or 'did' before the main verb for emphasis: to insist something is true, to contrast with what someone thinks, or to sound warm and sincere.
whenToUse: Contrast: 'I don't have a receipt, but I do have the email.'
Sincere politeness: 'I do apologise.' 'Do sit down.'

form.example: I do understand your frustration.
I did tell you about the storm.
Do come in.
I DID check the log.

examples: I do apologise for the inconvenience, Mr. Weller.
She does seem nervous today.
I did see Rafael near the drawer.
Do take a seat.

commonMistakes.wrong: Do you sit down. (as a polite invitation)

tips: 'I do apologise' sounds more sincere than 'I apologise' in customer service.
Use it to defend yourself calmly: 'I did follow the procedure.'

title: Whom and prepositions in relative clauses
explanation: In formal English, a preposition can go before 'whom' or 'which' (the person to whom...); in informal English it goes at the end (the person I spoke to). Wrong: 'the person to who I spoke', 'the room in which I stayed in'. Right: 'the person to whom I spoke' / 'the person I spoke to'.

lesson.whatItIs: When a verb has a preposition (speak to, rely on, stay in), the preposition can move in a relative clause. Formal English puts it before 'whom' (for people) or 'which' (for things). Everyday English leaves it at the end and often drops the relative pronoun.

form.example: the guest to whom I spoke
the villa in which the wedding took place
the guest (who) I spoke to
the colleague whom I trust
120 guests, most of whom were from Lagos

examples: The inspector, to whom I owe an apology, was very fair.
This is the evidence on which my report is based.
Mateo, whom everyone trusted, falsified the data.
We invited 120 guests, half of whom arrived by boat.

commonMistakes.wrong: the person to who I spoke
commonMistakes.right: the person to whom I spoke

commonMistakes.wrong: the room in which I stayed in
commonMistakes.right: the room in which I stayed / the room I stayed in
the person whom I spoke to / the person to whom I spoke

commonMistakes.wrong: 120 guests, most of them were from Lagos
commonMistakes.right: 120 guests, most of whom were from Lagos
commonMistakes.why: Joining clauses with commas needs 'of whom'.

tips: In chat, 'the guy I talked to' is perfectly natural; save 'to whom' for formal writing.
Never use 'that' after a preposition: 'the room in that I stayed' is wrong.

title: Advanced passives (being done / to be done / should have been done)
explanation: The passive can follow modals, appear as a gerund (being + past participle) or infinitive (to be + past participle), and in continuous and perfect forms. Wrong: 'I hate interrupting.' (meaning someone interrupts me) / 'It should have done earlier.' Right: 'I hate being interrupted.' / 'It should have been done earlier.'

lesson.whatItIs: Beyond 'is done' and 'was done', the passive can combine with almost any verb form: modals, gerunds, infinitives, continuous and perfect tenses. These forms let you focus on the action or result in complex sentences.
whenToUse: Saying what needs to happen without naming who
Talking about things done to you

form.example: The guests must be informed.
This should have been reported earlier.
Nobody likes being accused.
The lift needs to be repaired. I expect to be paid.
The room is being cleaned.
The invoice had already been sent.

form.pattern: need + -ing (= needs to be done, informal)
form.example: The generator needs fixing.

examples: The data should have been checked before upload.
Rafael denied being involved.
The ceremony is being moved to the boathouse.
The rings seem to have been hidden on purpose.

commonMistakes.wrong: I hate interrupting. (meaning: I am interrupted)

commonMistakes.right: It should have been done earlier.
The lift needs to be repaired. / The lift needs repairing.
The room is being cleaned now.
commonMistakes.why: Continuous passive → is being + past participle.

tips: 'Needs fixing' = 'needs to be fixed'; both are correct.
Use 'should have been + past participle' for polite formal criticism: 'The guest should have been informed.'

title: Reference words to avoid repetition (this / such / the former / the latter)
explanation: Refer back to earlier ideas with this/that/these/those, such + noun, the former/the latter, do so and one(s) instead of repeating words. Wrong: 'There was a power cut. The power cut caused panic.' Right: 'There was a power cut. This caused panic.'

lesson.whatItIs: Good writing connects sentences by pointing back to ideas already mentioned. Reference words refer to a previous noun, sentence or idea so you don't have to repeat it, which makes texts smoother and more professional.

form.pattern: this / these (+ noun) = an idea just mentioned
form.example: The generator failed. This meant we had no heating.

form.pattern: that / those (more distant, or in speech)
form.example: That was the worst night of the year.

form.pattern: such (+ a) + noun = of this type
form.example: Such behaviour is unacceptable.

form.pattern: the former (first of two) / the latter (second of two)
form.example: Plan A and Plan B are both risky; the latter is more expensive.

form.pattern: do so (replaces a verb phrase, formal)
form.example: Staff should report it and do so quickly.
the black bag, not the brown one

examples: Mateo falsified the data. This put the whole station at risk.
Such mistakes cannot happen again.
Amara and Daniel disagreed; the former wanted to move inside.
Grace offered to check the laundry, and she did so immediately.

commonMistakes.wrong: The lift stopped. The lift stopping caused panic.
commonMistakes.right: The lift stopped. This caused panic.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'this' to refer to the whole event.

commonMistakes.wrong: Kofi and Astrid agreed; the last wanted more fuel.
commonMistakes.right: Kofi and Astrid agreed; the latter wanted more fuel.
commonMistakes.why: For two items, use 'the former / the latter'.

tips: Add a noun after 'this' when it could be unclear: 'This decision caused...'
'The former / the latter' only work with exactly two items.
